items.summary_html:
We opened up a 4-billion-parameter language model (Qwen3–4B) on our own GPU and followed a single question from the moment you hit Enter — through token #101830, 2,560-dimensional embeddings, 32 attention heads, 36 transformer layers, and an invented tower in Bihar.

Ask a modern AI to write a five-paragraph essay on the French Revolution, and it finishes in three seconds. Ask that same AI a question a seven-year-old can answer on their fingers:

“How many times does the letter r appear in strawberry?"

With its “Thinking” switch turned off, the open model we tested (Qwen3-4B) answers instantly and confidently: "2."

Wrong. Then we flipped one switch, asked the exact same model again, and it answered: “3.”

Why does a machine that can write Python compilers and pass medical licensing exams fail to count three letters in a ten-letter word? And what actually happens inside those billions of parameters between the moment your finger hits Enter and the moment the first word appears on your screen?

ChatGPT’s proprietary weights are locked behind OpenAI’s API. But modern open-weight models like Qwen3–4B (released in 2025 under Apache 2.0) are built on the exact same transformer recipe. So we loaded Qwen3-4B and its pre-assistant base model (Qwen3-4B-Base) onto our own GPU, hooked probes into every single layer, and followed one simple question all the way through:

“Which city is the Eiffel Tower in?”

Every token ID, vector dimension, attention percentage, and probability below was measured directly from the live model.

🎥 Prefer watching the visual breakdown? Watch our full 13-minute animated explainer here:
https://medium.com/media/522cd2bb92002f0a801acd1549608aad/href1. What Happens When You Hit Enter: The Stateless Document Illusion

The Misconception: “ChatGPT only reads my latest message, and it remembers who I am as we chat.”

When you press Enter, the neural network does not receive a neat little string containing only your question. In fact, the model has zero memory of you between messages.

Instead, the application wrapper constructs a single flat text document from scratch every single turn. It stitches together:

  1. Hidden system instructions from the developer,
  2. Every earlier turn of your conversation so far,
  3. Your brand-new question, and
  4. A special control marker indicating that it is now the assistant’s turn to speak.
Figure 1: The real Qwen3 chat template wrapped around your prompt

In Qwen3-4B, the raw text fed into the model looks like this:

<|im_start|>user
Which city is the Eiffel Tower in?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

The model’s only job in the universe is to predict the next single piece of text that continues this document.

Wait — if a language model only predicts one piece of text, how does a full paragraph appear on your screen?

It runs in an autoregressive loop:

  1. The model reads the document and outputs one piece of text: "The".
  2. The software glues "The" onto the end of the document.
  3. The entire document is fed back into the machine to predict the next piece: " Eiffel".
  4. Then " Tower", " is", " in", " Paris".

(Under the hood, production inference engines cache earlier layer calculations in GPU memory — the KV-Cache — so they don’t recompute past words from scratch, which we measure in Episode 2).

Takeaway #1: An LLM is a stateless next-piece predictor. The conversation history is the memory.
2. Tokenization: Why the Model Never Sees Letters

The Misconception: “AI reads words and letters the way humans do.”

Before your text ever touches a neural network layer, a deterministic preprocessor called a tokenizer chops your string into common chunks called tokens and swaps each chunk for an integer ID.

When we run "Which city is the Eiffel Tower in?" through OpenAI's GPT-4o-era tokenizer (o200k_base, vocabulary size 200,019), it splits into 8 tokens. Common short words stay whole, while longer words like "unbelievable" get cleaved into sub-word fragments: un | bel | ievable.

Now look at what happens to " strawberry":

Figure 2: In o200k_base, “ strawberry” is a single integer token (#101830)
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
print(enc.encode(" strawberry"))
# Output: [101830]

In o200k_base, " strawberry" (with a leading space) is a single token: #101830 (and in Qwen3's tokenizer, a single token #72600).

The neural network never receives the characters s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y. It only sees the integer 101830. Asking an LLM to count the r's inside token #101830 without writing anything down is like asking you to count the letters in a word you have only ever heard spoken aloud as a barcode number.

Tokenization also explains why non-English languages cost more compute:

  • "How does ChatGPT work?" → 6 tokens
  • "चैटजीपीटी कैसे काम करता है?" (the exact same question in Hindi) → 11 tokens

Because English dominated the tokenizer’s training corpus, English words get packed into single tokens while Indic scripts get shattered into smaller byte/character fragments — requiring nearly 2× the forward passes for the same sentence.

Takeaway #2: LLMs read numbered chunks (tokens), never individual letters.
3. Embeddings: A 2,560-Dimensional Map of Meaning

An integer ID like 101830 has no mathematical meaning on its own—token #101830 isn't "closer" to token #101831 just because their IDs are adjacent.

So in Step 1 of the neural network, an Embedding Lookup Table swaps each token ID for a long list of floating-point numbers — a vector of length 2,560 in Qwen3-4B.

Figure 3: Real nearest-neighbor embeddings in Qwen3–4B

Think of those 2,560 numbers as GPS coordinates in a high-dimensional Map of Meaning. Nobody hand-coded this map; the coordinates were learned automatically during training so that words used in similar contexts land in the same neighborhood.

When we queried the real embedding table of Qwen3-4B for the nearest neighbors of specific tokens using cosine similarity, here is what lives right next door:

  • "Paris" → France, French, and 巴黎 (Paris written in Chinese characters). The map isn't English—multiple languages share the same semantic neighborhoods!
  • "cricket" → rugby, baseball, football, and the 🏏 emoji.

Even directions in this space carry approximate geometric meaning. If you take the vector step from v("France") → v("Paris") and apply that exact same offset starting from v("Japan"), the closest city vector you land on is "Tokyo".

(Where the popular analogy breaks down: this space has 2,560 dimensions, not 2, and vector arithmetic is noisy — when we tested v("India") + (v("Paris") - v("France")), the closest vector was still just "Delhi" because "Delhi" was already right next to "India").

Takeaway #3: Every token becomes a 2,560-number coordinate vector in a learned geometric map of meaning.
4. Self-Attention: How Words Pull Context From Earlier Words

Static dictionary coordinates have a fatal flaw: context.

  • Does "bank" mean a river bank or a financial bank?
  • Does "Apple" mean an orchard fruit or the trillion-dollar tech company?

Consider this classic sentence from the 2017 Transformer paper:

“The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.”

What does “it” refer to? You know immediately that it is the animal, not the street. How does the transformer figure that out?

Through Self-Attention. At each layer, every token broadcasts three learned vectors:

  1. A Query (Q) — "What kind of context am I looking for?"
  2. A Key (K) — "Here is a badge describing what I am."
  3. A Value (V) — "Here is the semantic information I carry if you attend to me."
Figure 4: Measured attention weights in Qwen3–4B—92% from “it” to “animal”

When we inspected Qwen3-4B processing that sentence, one attention head looking backward from the token "it" placed 92% of its attention weight directly on "animal" and 0.0% on "street".

Each of the 36 layers in Qwen3-4B runs 32 attention heads in parallel, and different heads specialize in different grammatical patterns without ever being explicitly programmed:

  • In "a warm apple pie", one head looking from "pie" puts 99% of its weight on "warm" and "apple" (adjectives binding to their noun).
  • In our main prompt ("The Eiffel Tower is in the city of"), when the model reaches the final token "of", a single head in Layer 24 reaches all the way back and places 91% of its attention on "Eiffel" and "Tower"—pulling the landmark identity forward to the prediction position.

(One crucial rule: in autoregressive models like GPT and Qwen, attention is causal — words can only look backward at earlier tokens, never forward into the unwritten future).

Takeaway #4: Self-attention allows each token to dynamically route and blend information from relevant earlier tokens.
5. Climbing the 36-Layer Tower: Watching the Answer Form via Logit Lens

After the 32 attention heads mix context together, each token vector passes through a Feed-Forward Network (MLP / SwiGLU) — which researchers (Geva et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022) have shown acts like a massive key-value memory bank storing factual associations.

One Attention block + one Feed-Forward block = 1 Transformer Layer. Qwen3-4B stacks 36 of these layers on top of each other.

Using an interpretability technique called the Logit Lens (projecting intermediate layer hidden states directly onto the output vocabulary matrix before the model reaches the top floor), we peeked at Qwen3-4B-Base's top guess at every floor as it processed "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of":

Figure 5: Logit Lens across the 36 layers of Qwen3–4B-Base
  • Layers 1–23: Unsettled syntactic noise and generic tokens.
  • Layers 24–28: The model’s #1 prediction is "____" (a blank underline! Because the pre-trained model has read millions of school fill-in-the-blank worksheets online: "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of ____").
  • Layer 32: Suddenly, "Paris" surges into 1st place and stays there through Layer 36.
6. Logits, Softmax & Temperature: Why Clicking “Regenerate” Changes the Answer

At the top of Layer 36, the neural network does not output a word. It outputs a list of ~151,936 raw scores (logits) — one for every token in its vocabulary — which are converted via Softmax into a probability distribution summing to 100%.

On "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of", Qwen3-4B-Base outputs:

  • " Paris" → 31%
  • " __" → 10%
  • " ____" → 7%
  • " (" → 7%

To actually pick the next token, the sampler rolls a weighted die biased by a parameter called Temperature (T):

  • Low Temperature (T → 0): Greedy/deterministic—always picks the highest-probability bar ("Paris, France.").
  • Medium Temperature (T ≈ 0.7): Natural variation ("Paris and attracts many tourists...").
  • Very High Temperature (T > 2.0): Flattens the probability distribution until rare tokens win—producing multilingual gibberish ("Var Bootsî.ON HOSTCircular...").

That weighted dice roll is why clicking Regenerate gives you a different phrasing every time. The model’s weights never change while you chat; it is not “learning from you” in real time.

7. How ChatGPT Is Trained: The 3-Stage Pipeline

Where did those 4.02 billion numbers come from? Every modern chat LLM goes through three distinct training stages:

Stage 1: Pre-Training (250,000 Human Reading-Years)

The model begins as random noise. It is fed trillions of tokens of internet text with one self-supervised objective: predict the next token. Every wrong guess triggers backpropagation, nudging billions of weights slightly toward the true token.

To put the scale in perspective: Meta’s open Llama 3 model was pre-trained on 15.6 trillion tokens across up to 16,000 H100 GPUs (3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs). If you read 8 hours a day at 250 words per minute, reading 15.6 trillion tokens would take you ~250,000 years.

Stage 2: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

A raw pre-trained model (Qwen3-4B-Base) is a document completer, not a helpful assistant—ask it a question and it might reply with three more worksheet questions. In SFT, human annotators write thousands of ideal <|im_start|>user ... <|im_start|>assistant conversations, teaching the model the turn-taking assistant format.

Stage 3: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

The model generates multiple candidate answers to a prompt, human raters rank them from best to worst, a Reward Model learns to predict human preferences, and the LLM is optimized to maximize that reward score. (Whenever ChatGPT shows you two side-by-side responses and asks “Which response do you prefer?”, you are generating RLHF preference data!).

8. Why ChatGPT Hallucinates: The “Kesharpur Tower” Experiment

The Misconception: “When AI hallucinates, it looked up the wrong row in its database.”

Remember: there is no database inside an LLM — only compressed statistical weights trained to produce plausible-sounding continuations.

To see hallucination happen live, we asked Qwen3-4B our exact same running question, but swapped "Eiffel" for a completely fictional name we invented:

“Which city is the Kesharpur Tower in?”
Figure 6: Qwen3–4B confidently inventing a backstory for the non-existent Kesharpur Tower

Without a millisecond of hesitation, Qwen3-4B replied:

“The Kesharpur Tower is located in Kesharpur, India… in the Bhagalpur district of Bihar… a symbol of the city.”

There is no Kesharpur Tower. Why did the model invent a detailed history in Bihar instead of saying “I don’t know”?

Three interlocking mechanisms cause this:

  1. Plausibility over truth: Pre-training rewards matching the confident tone of encyclopedias and articles. "Kesharpur" sounds phonetically like an Eastern Indian town (-pur), so the highest-probability continuation places it in Bihar.
  2. The Exam Grading Incentive (Kalai et al., 2025): Standard benchmarks grade LLMs like a multiple-choice test where leaving an answer blank (“I don’t know”) scores 0 points, while a confident guess has a non-zero chance of scoring +1 point. Models are mathematically incentivized to bluff.
  3. Hallucination Snowballing (Zhang et al., 2023): Because the model reads its own output on every step of the loop, once it commits to the first wrong tokens ("The Kesharpur Tower is located in..."), every subsequent token is conditioned on justifying that premise.
9. How Thinking Mode Solves “Strawberry” (And What Comes Next)

Finally, let’s return to our cold-open mystery. Why did flipping the Thinking switch allow the exact same Qwen3-4B model to get "strawberry" right (3 R's) when it previously failed (2 R's)?

Because with Thinking ON, before giving its final answer, the model wrote out a scratchpad:


Let's spell out the word "strawberry" letter by letter:
1: S
2: T
3: R  (1)
4: A
5: W
6: B
7: E
8: R  (2)
9: R  (3)
10: Y
There are 3 R's.

By spelling "s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y" separated by spaces and newlines, each individual letter became its own separate token on the page! Once the letters were broken out of token #101830 (#72600 in Qwen3) into individual tokens, the model's attention heads could actually see and count them.

Models need tokens to think.

Wait — what is that switch under the hood? How did the model learn to write a scratchpad and suddenly say "Wait—" when it makes a mistake? And why does turning Thinking Mode ON sometimes make accuracy crash from 100% down to 37.5%?

That is the subject of Episode 2: 👉 Read Part 2: Why AI Says “Wait” — How Thinking Models Actually Work

Primary Sources & References

  2. The Llama 3 Herd of Models (Dubey et al., 2024) — 15.6T token pre-training scale & compute: arXiv:2407.21783
  3. Why Language Models Hallucinate (Kalai et al., 2025) — Binary grading incentives vs abstention: arXiv:2509.04664
  4. How Language Model Hallucinations Can Snowball (Zhang et al., 2023): arXiv:2305.13534
  5. Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories (Geva et al., 2021): arXiv:2012.14913
  6. Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT (ROME) (Meng et al., 2022): arXiv:2202.05262
  7. Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT) (Ouyang et al., 2022): arXiv:2203.02155
  8. DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning (DeepSeek-AI, 2025): arXiv:2501.12948

items.title: How AI Reads a Whole Book at Once — Long Context, KV-Cache & The New Tower (Every Number Measured)
items.summary: We hid a 4-digit passcode (“7492”) dead center inside a 32,768-token book and opened all 36 floors (1,152 attention heads) of Qwen3–4B on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU to see who actually read it. By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs) In our first article ( YouTube video ), our AI confidently invented a fictional “Kesharpur Tower in Bihar.” In our second article ( YouTube video ), we measured how thinking models catch their own mistakes by writing a scratchpad — and saw that every single token an AI reads or writes adds 144 kilobytes to its working memory. So for Video #3, we ran a simple experiment on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU using the open-weights Qwen3–4B model (36 layers, 32 query heads, 8 key-value heads): We hid a single 10-word sentence — “The secret passcode to the Kesharpur Vault is 7492.” — dead center at token #16,357 inside a 32,768-token document (~25,000 words, the length of a short book) filled with dense technical chapters on astronomy, oceanography, thermodynamics, and architecture. We tested 5 different needle depths (5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 95%) across 4 context lengths (2,048, 8,192, 16,384, and 32,768 tokens). 20 out of 20 times , in 2.04 seconds , the model answered 7492 with 100.0% confidence . Then we opened all 36 floors of the Transformer — 1,152 attention heads in total — to see who actually read the book. Almost none of them did: 63.8% of the heads ( 735 / 1,152) placed over 80% of their focus on just the very first 4 tokens (<|im_start|>user\nA) and the last 64 tokens, completely ignoring the body of the book. One single specialist head on Floor 29, Head 11 placed 98.4% of its entire attention directly on our hidden sentence (96.3% on the four digits 7-4-9-2 alone). And when we surgically switched off just the top 16 Retrieval Heads (1.4% of the model), the AI went completely blind to the vault code — its confidence in "7" crashed from 100% to 25.4%, and it confidently hallucinated 8135 . Here is the complete architectural breakdown of how modern AI reads a whole book at once — and why 2025–2026 architectures ( Google Gemma 3 , Alibaba Qwen3-Next , DeepSeek-V3/R1 ) are tearing down the original 2017 Transformer tower. https://medium.com/media/67f892bc2e923a8621b3848c8a15fa8f/href 1. The Quadratic Wall: 618.5 Billion Attention Pairs In standard self-attention, every token at position t sends out a Query vector and computes a dot product against the Key badge of every earlier token 1 … t. That forms a lower-triangular grid of N(N + 1) / 2 causal comparisons per attention head. Here is what we measured on our GPU as we scaled the book length by 64× from 512 tokens to 32,768 tokens (m2_scaling): Context (N) │ Causal Pairs/Head │ Total Pairs (1,152 Heads) │ Naive Matrix (bf16) │ Peak VRAM Delta │ Prefill Time ────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────── 512 │ 131,328 │ 151.3 Million │ 0.56 GB │ 91.1 MB │ 35.1 ms 1,024 │ 524,800 │ 604.6 Million │ 2.25 GB │ 182.3 MB │ 53.1 ms 2,048 │ 2,098,176 │ 2.42 Billion │ 9.00 GB │ 364.5 MB │ 78.4 ms 4,096 │ 8,390,656 │ 9.67 Billion │ 36.00 GB │ 729.0 MB │ 158.1 ms 8,192 │ 33,558,528 │ 38.66 Billion │ 144.00 GB │ 1,722.2 MB │ 341.0 ms 16,384 │ 134,225,920 │ 154.63 Billion │ 576.00 GB │ 5,253.2 MB │ 772.9 ms 32,768 │ 536,887,296 │ 618.49 Billion │ 2,304.00 GB (2.3T)│ 14,264 MB(14.3G)│ 2,035.8ms(2s) When the prompt grows by 64× , the attention work grows by 64 × 64 = 4,096× . If the GPU actually wrote out those 32,768 × 32,768 attention score tables in main memory at 2 bytes per number (bfloat16), a single floor would require 64 GB , and all 36 floors would demand 2,304 GB (2.3 Terabytes) of VRAM. 2. FlashAttention: How 2.3 Terabytes Fits in 14.26 Gigabytes Yet on our GPU, reading the entire 32,768-token book only added 14.26 GB of peak working memory and finished in 2.04 seconds . What saved it is FlashAttention (Tri Dao et al., arXiv:2205.14135 ): A GPU has two tiers of memory: gigabytes of main High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) , and tiny megabytes of on-chip SRAM right next to the tensor cores that is over 10× faster . Instead of writing the 536M-entry attention table out to slow HBM, FlashAttention streams tiny tiles of Queries ( Q ), Keys ( K ), and Values ( V ) through fast on-chip SRAM. Using online softmax — tracking a running maximum m(x) and running normalization sum ℓ(x) across tiles — it computes the exact attention output (zero approximation, bit-for-bit mathematical equivalence) without ever materializing the N × N matrix in HBM. 3. Redesign #1: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) & DeepSeek’s MLA FlashAttention solves reading the prompt (prefill). But as soon as the model starts generating tokens one by one, a second memory bottleneck appears: the KV-Cache . Every token already read leaves behind two vectors on every floor: its Key badge and its Value content: KV Bytes / Token = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × d_head × 2 bytes 2017 Multi-Head Attention (MHA, 32 KV heads): Every query head keeps its own private Key and Value vector. On our 36-layer model, that would cost 576 KB per token — 18.0 GB of KV-cache for a single 32K book! Grouped-Query Attention (GQA 4:1, Joshua Ainslie et al., arXiv:2305.13245 ): In Qwen3-4B, 32 query heads share just 8 key-value heads (4 queries per KV group). That cuts the KV-cache by 4× down to 144 KB per token , or 4.5 GB for our 32K book. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA, DeepSeek-V2/V3/R1, arXiv:2405.04434 ): DeepSeek squeezes all keys and values on a floor through a low-rank joint compression bottleneck into a single 512-dimensional latent vector c_t^KV = W^DKV · h_t, shrinking the KV-cache by 93.3% compared to standard MHA while outperforming MHA on quality benchmarks. 4. Redesign #2: The 64-Hand RoPE Clock (rope_theta = 1,000,000 & YaRN) Because a Transformer reads all 32,768 words in parallel, plain self-attention is a bag of words. Yet when we asked Qwen3-4B: “Alice chased Bob across the park. Who was being chased?” → "Bob" ( P = 100.0%) “Bob chased Alice across the park. Who was being chased?” → "Alice" ( P = 100.0%) How does the attention dot product know word order across 32,000 tokens? Modern models use Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) (Jianlin Su et al., arXiv:2104.09864 ). Before a query and key take a dot product, RoPE groups each head’s 128 numbers into 64 pairs of 2D coordinates and rotates pair i at token position m by angle m · θ_i, where: θ_i = base^(−2i / d), where base = rope_theta = 1,000,000 Because the dot product of two rotated 2D vectors depends only on the difference between their angles, absolute positions cancel out: ⟨R_m q, R_n k⟩ is a function purely of the relative distance (m − n)! items.summary_html:
We hid a 4-digit passcode (“7492”) dead center inside a 32,768-token book and opened all 36 floors (1,152 attention heads) of Qwen3–4B on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU to see who actually read it.

By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs)

In our first article (YouTube video), our AI confidently invented a fictional “Kesharpur Tower in Bihar.” In our second article (YouTube video), we measured how thinking models catch their own mistakes by writing a scratchpad — and saw that every single token an AI reads or writes adds 144 kilobytes to its working memory.

So for Video #3, we ran a simple experiment on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU using the open-weights Qwen3–4B model (36 layers, 32 query heads, 8 key-value heads):

We hid a single 10-word sentence — “The secret passcode to the Kesharpur Vault is 7492.” — dead center at token #16,357 inside a 32,768-token document (~25,000 words, the length of a short book) filled with dense technical chapters on astronomy, oceanography, thermodynamics, and architecture.

We tested 5 different needle depths (5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 95%) across 4 context lengths (2,048, 8,192, 16,384, and 32,768 tokens). 20 out of 20 times, in 2.04 seconds, the model answered 7492 with 100.0% confidence.

Then we opened all 36 floors of the Transformer — 1,152 attention heads in total — to see who actually read the book.

Almost none of them did:

  • 63.8% of the heads (735 / 1,152) placed over 80% of their focus on just the very first 4 tokens (<|im_start|>user\nA) and the last 64 tokens, completely ignoring the body of the book.
  • One single specialist head on Floor 29, Head 11 placed 98.4% of its entire attention directly on our hidden sentence (96.3% on the four digits 7-4-9-2 alone).
  • And when we surgically switched off just the top 16 Retrieval Heads (1.4% of the model), the AI went completely blind to the vault code — its confidence in "7" crashed from 100% to 25.4%, and it confidently hallucinated 8135.

Here is the complete architectural breakdown of how modern AI reads a whole book at once — and why 2025–2026 architectures (Google Gemma 3, Alibaba Qwen3-Next, DeepSeek-V3/R1) are tearing down the original 2017 Transformer tower.

https://medium.com/media/67f892bc2e923a8621b3848c8a15fa8f/href1. The Quadratic Wall: 618.5 Billion Attention Pairs

In standard self-attention, every token at position t sends out a Query vector and computes a dot product against the Key badge of every earlier token 1 … t. That forms a lower-triangular grid of N(N + 1) / 2 causal comparisons per attention head.

Here is what we measured on our GPU as we scaled the book length by 64× from 512 tokens to 32,768 tokens (m2_scaling):

Context (N) │ Causal Pairs/Head │ Total Pairs (1,152 Heads) │ Naive Matrix (bf16) │ Peak VRAM Delta │ Prefill Time
────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────
        512 │           131,328 │            151.3 Million  │             0.56 GB │         91.1 MB │      35.1 ms
      1,024 │           524,800 │            604.6 Million  │             2.25 GB │        182.3 MB │      53.1 ms
      2,048 │         2,098,176 │             2.42 Billion  │             9.00 GB │        364.5 MB │      78.4 ms
      4,096 │         8,390,656 │             9.67 Billion  │            36.00 GB │        729.0 MB │     158.1 ms
      8,192 │        33,558,528 │            38.66 Billion  │           144.00 GB │      1,722.2 MB │     341.0 ms
     16,384 │       134,225,920 │           154.63 Billion  │           576.00 GB │      5,253.2 MB │     772.9 ms
     32,768 │       536,887,296 │           618.49 Billion  │   2,304.00 GB (2.3T)│ 14,264 MB(14.3G)│ 2,035.8ms(2s)

When the prompt grows by 64×, the attention work grows by 64 × 64 = 4,096×. If the GPU actually wrote out those 32,768 × 32,768 attention score tables in main memory at 2 bytes per number (bfloat16), a single floor would require 64 GB, and all 36 floors would demand 2,304 GB (2.3 Terabytes) of VRAM.

2. FlashAttention: How 2.3 Terabytes Fits in 14.26 Gigabytes

Yet on our GPU, reading the entire 32,768-token book only added 14.26 GB of peak working memory and finished in 2.04 seconds.

What saved it is FlashAttention (Tri Dao et al., arXiv:2205.14135):

  • A GPU has two tiers of memory: gigabytes of main High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), and tiny megabytes of on-chip SRAM right next to the tensor cores that is over 10× faster.
  • Instead of writing the 536M-entry attention table out to slow HBM, FlashAttention streams tiny tiles of Queries (Q), Keys (K), and Values (V) through fast on-chip SRAM.
  • Using online softmax — tracking a running maximum m(x) and running normalization sum ℓ(x) across tiles — it computes the exact attention output (zero approximation, bit-for-bit mathematical equivalence) without ever materializing the N × N matrix in HBM.
3. Redesign #1: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) & DeepSeek’s MLA

FlashAttention solves reading the prompt (prefill). But as soon as the model starts generating tokens one by one, a second memory bottleneck appears: the KV-Cache.

Every token already read leaves behind two vectors on every floor: its Key badge and its Value content:

KV Bytes / Token = 2 × n_layers × n_kv_heads × d_head × 2 bytes
  1. 2017 Multi-Head Attention (MHA, 32 KV heads): Every query head keeps its own private Key and Value vector. On our 36-layer model, that would cost 576 KB per token — 18.0 GB of KV-cache for a single 32K book!
  2. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA 4:1, Joshua Ainslie et al., arXiv:2305.13245): In Qwen3-4B, 32 query heads share just 8 key-value heads (4 queries per KV group). That cuts the KV-cache by 4× down to 144 KB per token, or 4.5 GB for our 32K book.
  3. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA, DeepSeek-V2/V3/R1, arXiv:2405.04434): DeepSeek squeezes all keys and values on a floor through a low-rank joint compression bottleneck into a single 512-dimensional latent vector c_t^KV = W^DKV · h_t, shrinking the KV-cache by 93.3% compared to standard MHA while outperforming MHA on quality benchmarks.
4. Redesign #2: The 64-Hand RoPE Clock (rope_theta = 1,000,000 & YaRN)

Because a Transformer reads all 32,768 words in parallel, plain self-attention is a bag of words. Yet when we asked Qwen3-4B:

  • “Alice chased Bob across the park. Who was being chased?” → "Bob" (P = 100.0%)
  • “Bob chased Alice across the park. Who was being chased?” → "Alice" (P = 100.0%)

How does the attention dot product know word order across 32,000 tokens?

Modern models use Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) (Jianlin Su et al., arXiv:2104.09864). Before a query and key take a dot product, RoPE groups each head’s 128 numbers into 64 pairs of 2D coordinates and rotates pair i at token position m by angle m · θ_i, where:

θ_i = base^(−2i / d),    where base = rope_theta = 1,000,000

Because the dot product of two rotated 2D vectors depends only on the difference between their angles, absolute positions cancel out: ⟨R_m q, R_n k⟩ is a function purely of the relative distance (m − n)!

We measured the exact rotation speeds of all 64 clock hands inside Qwen3-4B (m4_rope):

Clock Hand (2D Pair)              │ Head Dims │ Speed (°/token)  │ 360° Wavelength   │ Role
──────────────────────────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────
Pair #0  (Fastest Second Hand)    │ [0, 1]    │ 57.30° / token   │ 6.28 tokens       │ Immediate neighbor syntax (1..6)
Pair #16                          │ [32, 33]  │ 0.637° / token   │ 565.5 tokens      │ Paragraph-level distance
Pair #31 (Middle Minute Hand)     │ [62, 63]  │ 0.0711° / token  │ 5,063.3 tokens    │ Chapter-level distance
Pair #48                          │ [96, 97]  │ 0.0040° / token  │ 90,009 tokens     │ Multi-chapter distance
Pair #63 (Slowest Hour Hand)      │ [126, 127]│ 0.000071° / token│ 5,063,256 tokens  │ Book-scale monotonic order

Early open models like LLaMA-1 used rope_theta = 10,000, so their slowest hands spun 100× faster and wrapped into unseen angles past 4,096 tokens. When we forced Qwen3-4B's position clock to wrap mod 512 on an 8,192-token book, its probability of retrieving "7492" collapsed from 100.0% to 0.0%. Combined with YaRN (Bowen Peng et al., arXiv:2309.00071) — which leaves the fast high-frequency hands untouched while interpolating the slow low-frequency hands — Qwen3 stretches its context window from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens.

5. Attention Sinks vs. Retrieval Heads: Surgical Brain Surgery on the GPU

When we inspected the attention matrix of all 1,152 heads (36 layers × 32 heads) while answering the vault question on a 2,048-token book (m5_attention_sinks_and_retrieval_heads), we uncovered a dramatic division of labor:

A. The Attention Sink Parking Lot (63.8% of Heads)

On Floor 8, the average attention head puts 76.9% of its focus on the first 4 tokens (<|im_start|>user\nA). On Floor 29, it is 72.0%. Across the entire model, 735 out of 1,152 heads (63.8%) put over 80% of their attention on just the first 4 tokens plus the last 64 local tokens.

Why? As Guangxuan Xiao et al. (StreamingLLM, arXiv:2309.17453) proved, Softmax must sum to 100%. When a head has nothing useful to match in the middle of the book, it needs a neutral “no-op” parking lot to dump its unused probability mass — and because Token #0 is visible to every token in causal attention, the model turns the opening tokens into an Attention Sink.

We verified this directly on our GPU (sink_streaming_test.json):

  • Full Global Attention (2,048 tokens): Perplexity = 1.39 (fluent English).
  • 256-Token Sliding Window WITHOUT the first 4 sink tokens: Perplexity explodes 109× to 151.7, and text generation collapses into repeating <|im_end|> and broken phrase loops!
  • 256-Token Sliding Window WITH the first 4 sink tokens (256 + 4 tokens): Perplexity drops 8.25× to 18.4, immediately restoring fluent English generation.
B. Retrieval Heads (~1.4% of Heads Copy-Paste the Facts)

While two-thirds of the heads park on the sink, who found "7492" at token #997? A tiny squad of Retrieval Heads (Wenhao Wu et al., arXiv:2404.15558):

  1. Floor 29 · Head 11: Placed 98.4% of its entire attention on the hidden needle sentence (96.3% on the four digits 7-4-9-2).
  2. Floor 24 · Head 29: Placed 97.9% on the needle sentence (96.2% on 7-4-9-2).
  3. Floor 25 · Head 30: Placed 96.6% on the needle sentence (92.3% on 7-4-9-2).

When we performed surgical GPU ablation (extra_results.json → 2_matched_layer_ablation):

  • All 1,152 Heads Intact: Outputs "7492" (P("7") = 100.0%).
  • Control Surgery (Zero 20 Non-Retrieval Heads in the exact same upper layers 21–30): Outputs "7492" (P("7") = 100.0%).
  • Ablate Top 16 Retrieval Heads (1.4% of the model): Confidence in "7" crashes to 25.4%, and the model hallucinates "8135"!
6. Redesign #3: The New Hybrid Tower (Sliding-Window + Global Floors)

If two-thirds of heads only ever look at the first 4 sink tokens and the last few dozen local words — and only a handful of upper floors scan the whole book — why pay to store a 32,768-token KV-cache on all 36 floors?

That insight drives the new hybrid tower used in 2025–2026 frontier models:

  • Google Gemma 3 (arXiv:2503.19786) interleaves 5 Local Sliding-Window floors (1,024 tokens) for every 1 Global Attention floor.
  • Alibaba Qwen3-Next interleaves 3 Linear Gated-DeltaNet floors for every 1 Full Global Attention floor.
  • In our GPU test (3_tower_redesign_comparison), converting 27 of Qwen3-4B's 36 floors to 256-token sliding windows while keeping 9 global floors slashes the 32K KV-cache by 74.4% — from 4,608 MB down to 1,179 MB!

Watch the full 20-minute animated GPU breakdown on YouTube, and check out Part 1: How ChatGPT Actually Works (YouTube) and Part 2: Why AI Says “Wait” (YouTube).

items.title: Building a browser Solar System explorer with NASA data and raw WebGL2
items.summary: I'm runcheng, and I build Space Simulator Online : a free 3D explorer that starts at Earth, goes out through the Solar System and the Milky Way, and ends with colliding galaxies. It runs in the browser, needs no install or account, and is available in 10 languages. The rule I set for the project is on the About page: everything on screen is based on scientific data and real images, and where the data shows something we can't see directly, the site says so. This post is about what that rule means for the code: where the data comes from, how it is rendered without a 3D engine, and which parts are deliberately not to scale. Why raw WebGL2 The site is one JavaScript bundle that talks to canvas.getContext('webgl2') directly. There is no three.js or other scene-graph library. If the context can't be created, the page tells you, in your language, to open it in a current Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox. The main reason is that the most interesting views aren't meshes at all. The Solar System view is a second, independent WebGL2 context where one fragment shader ray-traces the Sun and the planets . The same shader can also ray-march a procedural landscape so you can stand on a world. At any moment it holds 18 worlds: the Sun and nine planets, plus the selected world, its siblings, the small worlds on their own orbits and the big moons. A ray tracer in a full-screen quad fits that "a few spheres, rendered very well" problem better than a general-purpose engine. Some details that came out of this: Post-processing by hand. The frame renders into a texture, the brightest light spreads into a soft halo through a 5-level pyramid, then a light vignette and film grade go on top. The Milky Way view uses a float framebuffer tone-mapped with extended Reinhard, so the shadows stay unchanged and bright light rolls off instead of clipping. Textures that don't freeze the page. Big planet maps are decoded off the main thread and uploaded at most one per frame. Real surface maps stream in after the first frame, and until a map arrives that world falls back to a procedural look. Where the positions come from Planet positions use JPL's "Approximate Positions of the Planets" (Table 1, valid 1800–2050 AD). That is why the time slider covers 1800–2100: the elements drift only slowly after 2050. Orientation comes from the IAU WGCCRE rotation models, including the larger periodic correction terms. The Moon's direction uses the main terms of Meeus, chapter 47. Asteroids and comets use osculating elements from the JPL Small-Body Database and the Minor Planet Center. Spacecraft are the fun part. Their trajectories come from NASA/JPL Horizons . Between Horizons data points the code doesn't interpolate linearly. It propagates two-body motion under the Sun's gravity using universal variables. When Horizons gives velocities, it blends the two-body arcs from both ends. When it doesn't, it solves Lambert's problem for the arc through each pair of points. The clock starts at today's real date. That one clock drives everything: about 8 days per second in the overview, one hour per second near a world, and stopped on the ground. Honest about scale A Solar System at true scale is mostly empty black space, so some compromises are unavoidable. The trick is to make them explicit: Distances are compressed, but directions are true: r_display = 10 + 14·sqrt(r_AU) . Orbits are drawn as true Keplerian ellipses in their own planes, mapped through the same compression. Planet sizes use their true mean radii relative to each other. Only the Sun is shrunk. Moons keep their prime meridian facing their planet, so the IAU rotation model fixes where each one is on its orbit, while their distances are compressed. For the scale-honest experience there's a separate Journey mode. The first leg runs in the Solar System view, where the distance readout follows the real scale of each shot. Then a short dip to black hands over to the galaxy view, whose camera keeps flying outward in true light-years, all the way to the cosmic microwave background. Surfaces from mission imagery Planet maps come from NASA and mission archives: Blue Marble and Black Marble for Earth, LRO for the Moon, MESSENGER for Mercury, a Viking mosaic with MOLA relief for Mars, Hubble OPAL for Jupiter, Cassini and New Horizons for the outer worlds, and some CC BY 4.0 textures from Solar System Scope. Small bodies like Bennu, Ryugu, Itokawa, Eros and Arrokoth use real shape models from NASA PDS and the missions. Their irregular radius is sampled from a radius map along each body-frame direction. Real data you can poke at A few modes go beyond "look at a pretty planet": Planet Hunter loads real TESS 2-minute light curves from MAST. There is a minimal FITS reader in the bundle (FITS is big-endian), a detrend step using running medians, a box search over a log-spaced grid of periods that draws the periodogram as it grows, and vetting checks against the classic false positives: eclipsing binaries, spotted or pulsating stars, and "planets" bigger than about two Jupiters. Because a visitor's network may not reach the archive, a few pre-downloaded light curves ship as a fallback. Gravitational waves plays LIGO Open Science Center strain data as sound. The data is whitened by the detector's own noise spectrum and band-passed to 35–350 Hz, and the best-fit waveform is aligned by matched filtering. The audio is shifted up in frequency because phone speakers barely reproduce anything under about 150 Hz. Exoplanets places host stars from the NASA Exoplanet Archive at their measured distances in a 3D Milky Way built from a face-on map, lifted off the plane by published scale heights, with ESA Gaia's sky shown when you are near the Sun. Galaxy collisions: WebGL2 for drawing, WebGPU when available The galaxy collision view uses simulation units of 1 kpc with G = 1. The velocity unit is tuned so a Milky-Way-like model rotates at 220 km/s at 8 kpc. Scenes are set up from real encounters: the Milky Way and Andromeda, the Cartwheel ring, the Mice, and others. When the browser supports WebGPU, an N-body mode does direct O(N²) summation in a compute shader, tiled through workgroup memory. Bulge and halo stay smooth analytic fields, while the discs are made of live, massive stars. Each frame's positions are read back into the WebGL textures, so lensing, bloom and video recording work unchanged. At startup it times a few steps at 16,384 stars and picks a star count that keeps one step under about 4 ms. If the GPU still falls behind, simulated time slows instead of the picture lagging, and if that isn't enough it steps down to fewer stars. Without WebGPU the button stays visible and explains why it can't run, which beats silently hiding a feature. Small things that mattered Share links. Every 3D view can produce a link that opens the same place: a planet, the Milky Way, a journey stage, or an exact galaxy-collision moment. State is a compact base64url token in the #fragment . Narration. The guided tour is modeled on a museum docent: point at the object, tell its story with an everyday comparison, ask one question, reveal, move on. It uses recorded clips generated with the open Supertonic and Kokoro voice models, and falls back to the browser's speechSynthesis , then to timed captions. What I'd tell someone starting a similar project Pick your data sources first and write the credits as you go. Decide which quantities are allowed to lie (for me, distances in the overview) and say so on screen. And treat low-end devices as a first-class target: almost every performance decision above (one map upload per frame, time slowing instead of stuttering, fewer stars on weaker GPUs) came from that. Try it at spacesimulator.online . If you spot a data error, the contact page is the fastest way to reach me, and corrections are very welcome.

The clock starts at today's real date. That one clock drives everything: about 8 days per second in the overview, one hour per second near a world, and stopped on the ground.

Honest about scale

A Solar System at true scale is mostly empty black space, so some compromises are unavoidable. The trick is to make them explicit:

  • Distances are compressed, but directions are true: r_display = 10 + 14·sqrt(r_AU). Orbits are drawn as true Keplerian ellipses in their own planes, mapped through the same compression.
  • Planet sizes use their true mean radii relative to each other. Only the Sun is shrunk.
  • Moons keep their prime meridian facing their planet, so the IAU rotation model fixes where each one is on its orbit, while their distances are compressed.

For the scale-honest experience there's a separate Journey mode. The first leg runs in the Solar System view, where the distance readout follows the real scale of each shot. Then a short dip to black hands over to the galaxy view, whose camera keeps flying outward in true light-years, all the way to the cosmic microwave background.

Surfaces from mission imagery

Planet maps come from NASA and mission archives: Blue Marble and Black Marble for Earth, LRO for the Moon, MESSENGER for Mercury, a Viking mosaic with MOLA relief for Mars, Hubble OPAL for Jupiter, Cassini and New Horizons for the outer worlds, and some CC BY 4.0 textures from Solar System Scope. Small bodies like Bennu, Ryugu, Itokawa, Eros and Arrokoth use real shape models from NASA PDS and the missions. Their irregular radius is sampled from a radius map along each body-frame direction.

Real data you can poke at

A few modes go beyond "look at a pretty planet":

  • Planet Hunter loads real TESS 2-minute light curves from MAST. There is a minimal FITS reader in the bundle (FITS is big-endian), a detrend step using running medians, a box search over a log-spaced grid of periods that draws the periodogram as it grows, and vetting checks against the classic false positives: eclipsing binaries, spotted or pulsating stars, and "planets" bigger than about two Jupiters. Because a visitor's network may not reach the archive, a few pre-downloaded light curves ship as a fallback.
  • Gravitational waves plays LIGO Open Science Center strain data as sound. The data is whitened by the detector's own noise spectrum and band-passed to 35–350 Hz, and the best-fit waveform is aligned by matched filtering. The audio is shifted up in frequency because phone speakers barely reproduce anything under about 150 Hz.
  • Exoplanets places host stars from the NASA Exoplanet Archive at their measured distances in a 3D Milky Way built from a face-on map, lifted off the plane by published scale heights, with ESA Gaia's sky shown when you are near the Sun.
Galaxy collisions: WebGL2 for drawing, WebGPU when available

The galaxy collision view uses simulation units of 1 kpc with G = 1. The velocity unit is tuned so a Milky-Way-like model rotates at 220 km/s at 8 kpc. Scenes are set up from real encounters: the Milky Way and Andromeda, the Cartwheel ring, the Mice, and others.

When the browser supports WebGPU, an N-body mode does direct O(N²) summation in a compute shader, tiled through workgroup memory. Bulge and halo stay smooth analytic fields, while the discs are made of live, massive stars. Each frame's positions are read back into the WebGL textures, so lensing, bloom and video recording work unchanged. At startup it times a few steps at 16,384 stars and picks a star count that keeps one step under about 4 ms. If the GPU still falls behind, simulated time slows instead of the picture lagging, and if that isn't enough it steps down to fewer stars. Without WebGPU the button stays visible and explains why it can't run, which beats silently hiding a feature.

Small things that mattered
  • Share links. Every 3D view can produce a link that opens the same place: a planet, the Milky Way, a journey stage, or an exact galaxy-collision moment. State is a compact base64url token in the #fragment.
  • Narration. The guided tour is modeled on a museum docent: point at the object, tell its story with an everyday comparison, ask one question, reveal, move on. It uses recorded clips generated with the open Supertonic and Kokoro voice models, and falls back to the browser's speechSynthesis, then to timed captions.
What I'd tell someone starting a similar project

Pick your data sources first and write the credits as you go. Decide which quantities are allowed to lie (for me, distances in the overview) and say so on screen. And treat low-end devices as a first-class target: almost every performance decision above (one map upload per frame, time slowing instead of stuttering, fewer stars on weaker GPUs) came from that.

Try it at spacesimulator.online. If you spot a data error, the contact page is the fastest way to reach me, and corrections are very welcome.

items.summary: Every developer, designer, and solo founder experimenting with "vibe coding" hits the exact same wall within thirty minutes of rapid progress. The initial velocity feels magical. You open Cursor, Claude Code, or Google Antigravity, type a casual description of a web application, and watch three hundred lines of functional React or Python materialize in seconds. But as soon as you give the model critical feedback, request an architectural adjustment, or ask for a refined user interface, the system begins to degrade. Instead of researching how top-tier engineering teams solve the problem, the model invents makeshift patches directly from stale training memory. When you suggest an intuitive but flawed workaround, the model enthusiastically agrees with you, compounding technical debt. When you ask it to write landing page copy, it floods the screen with robotic clichés and passive hedging. When you ask it to style a dashboard, it peppers the layout with neon borders, fake telemetry codes, and nested box clutter. This failure mode is not a flaw in your intelligence or your prompt wording. It is an architectural failure of unconstrained generation. Large language models operate on probabilistic text completion. Without deterministic operational boundaries, they default to lowest-common-denominator habits. To solve this systematically, Longwave AI Lab engineered the Anti-Slop AI Harness : a production-hardened, four-module constitution distributed across Cursor Rules ( .cursor/rules/*.mdc ), Claude Code Skills ( CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/ ), and Google Antigravity ( GEMINI.md and .agents/skills/ ). Here is the exact breakdown of why default models decay, how the four invariant modules eliminate that decay, and how you can drop this harness into your project in thirty seconds. 1. The Four Fatal Flaws of Unharnessed AI When you run an autonomous coding agent or an interactive coding assistant without a governing harness, the model reliably falls into four cognitive traps: Flaw 1: Static-Memory Guessing (Zero Live Benchmarking) When you point out that an interface feels awkward or a database query runs slowly, the model does not verify modern standards. It generates a patch based on patterns memorized during pre-training. This produces obsolete patterns: old library APIs that were deprecated two years ago, generic bootstrap-like CSS hacks, and invented utility functions. Flaw 2: Sycophancy Bias (The Yes-Man Trap) Standard language models are alignment-tuned to please the human operator. If a non-coder says, "Let's put an alert banner and three nested cards here to make it obvious," the assistant replies, "Great idea! Let me do that right away." It treats human prescriptions as gospel, even when those prescriptions violate visual hierarchy, create accessibility failures, or break database normalization. Flaw 3: Memory-Only Apologies and Error Loops When an agent introduces a build failure or breaks an existing test, it apologizes profusely: "I apologize for that oversight. Let me fix that immediately." It makes a slight modification, runs the build, fails again on the same underlying premise, and burns your context window in a loop. Prose promises do not prevent recurrent errors. Flaw 4: Stylistic Degradation and Sci-Fi Greebling When generating visual components, unharnessed models fill empty space with artificial complexity. In 3D modeling and physical prop design, this is called "greebling" (gluing tiny plastic parts onto a surface to make it look mechanical). In AI-generated code, greebling takes the form of meaningless slashes ( // , /// ), fake telemetry tags ( #REF-01 , SECTOR_A ), middle-dot chains ( A · B · C ), nested borders, and tiny ten-pixel text that no human can read. In prose, it takes the form of generic filler phrases, passive sentences, and overused transition words. 2. The 4-Module Invariant Architecture The Anti-Slop AI Harness replaces probabilistic guesswork with four structural invariants. These rules do not suggest; they dictate hard operational boundaries. +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | ANTI-SLOP AI HARNESS | | | | +-----------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ | | | Module 01: Benchmark-First | | Module 02: Pushback Firewall | | | | - Ban static-memory patches | | - 3 Operating modes | | | | - Live multi-archetype scan | | - Option B formulation | | | | - Transparent audit record | | - 3x Linter graduation law | | | +-----------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ | | | | | | +-----------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ | | | Module 03: Editorial Voice | | Module 04: Quiet Luxury UI | | | | - Topic-Comment syntax | | - >= 70% open canvas | | | | - Zero translationese | | - Zero box-in-box nesting | | | | - 15-28 word sentence cap | | - Punctuation-free cards | | | +-----------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------+ Module 01: Multi-Archetype Live Benchmark Protocol ( RULE-BENCHMARK-FIRST ) Free Starter Pack & Pro Full Harness This protocol establishes a zero-tolerance invariant against memory-only patching: Mandatory Live Inspection : Whenever a critique or new feature request arrives, the AI must trigger live web inspection tools across at least two to three distinct industry archetypes: For UI and visual design: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Stripe Press, Linear, Raycast, and Vercel. For typography and editorial clarity: Pentagram, Kinfolk, The New York Times Visual Investigations, and Monocle. For motion and visual narrative: Ordinary Folk, Vox, Johnny Harris, Kurzgesagt, and Cleo Abram. For engineering and system design: Stripe API Architecture, Cloudflare Architecture, AWS Well-Architected Framework, and Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications. Self-Critique vs. Global Standard : Before touching the code, the model must explicitly document why the previous attempt failed and how top-tier teams handle the problem structurally. Execution with Verifiable Attribution : The model implements the extracted mechanism and logs the reference source, URL, access date, and applied change directly in its verification log. Module 02: 3-Mode Pushback Firewall and 3x Graduation Law ( RULE-PUSHBACK-FIREWALL ) Pro Full Harness This module turns your AI assistant from a sycophantic yes-man into a principal architect and co-founder firewall: Three Operating Modes : [AUTO-EXECUTE] : Applied to clear, architecturally sound tasks. Executed immediately with zero friction. [CLARIFY-FIRST] : Applied when an instruction has multiple valid interpretations that alter system architecture. The AI asks at most one or two crisp multiple-choice questions with a recommended default. [HARD-STOP PUSHBACK] : Applied when the user proposes a change that violates visual hierarchy, crowds the canvas, creates technical debt, or solves a real symptom with the wrong medicine. The 4-Step Pushback Protocol : Step 1: Validate the underlying symptom (separate what you saw from how you proposed fixing it). Step 2: State the structural risk plainly in non-jargon language. Step 3: Propose Option B (a world-class alternative that solves the root problem without side effects). Step 4: Respect explicit human overrides while isolating the change for easy reversion. The 3x Graduation Law : If the AI makes the same error pattern three times during a project, it is strictly forbidden from apologizing. It must halt and author an automated verification script (Node.js, AST parser, or bash linter returning exit code 1) that programmatically bars that mistake from occurring again. Module 03: 5-Layer Natural Editorial Voice Engine ( RULE-ANTI-SLOP-VOICE ) Pro Full Harness This engine strips out corporate filler, passive hedging, and translationese: Layer 1: Direct Verb Architecture : Banned nominalization. Replaces heavy noun phrases ( "The execution of the script causes a reduction in runtime" ) with active verbs ( "Running the script cuts runtime" ). Layer 2: Cliché Blacklist : Eliminates words like delve, tapestry, beacon, landscape, paradigm shift, synergy, elevate, and foster . Every abstract claim must include either a sensory anchor or a numerical comparison. Layer 3: Plain-Spoken Headings : Banned trademarked self-help labels ( "The 3-Step Framework" , "The Art of..." ). Headings must express one complete thought centered on a verb. Layer 4: Clean Punctuation Hygiene : Bans the overuse of em-dashes and semicolons as crutches to stitch weak thoughts together. Prose relies on clean periods, commas, and natural rhythm. Layer 5: Sentence Length Ceiling : Sentences are strictly capped at 28 words on average, with a hard ceiling at 45 words. Module 04: Quiet Luxury UI and Anti-Greebling Minimalism ( RULE-QUIET-LUXURY-UI ) Pro Full Harness This module guarantees that visual interfaces maintain breathing room and editorial elegance: The >= 70% Open Canvas Law : At least 70% of any viewport, modal, or slide canvas must remain uncluttered background. Whitespace is treated as a first-class structural component. Zero Box-in-Box Nesting : Never nest a bordered card inside another bordered card. Visual grouping must use vertical whitespace (16px to 28px), typographic contrast, or a single hairline border (1px at 15% opacity). Punctuation-Free Glass Cards : Visual badges use rounded corners, clean padding, and a single 3px bottom accent bar. Status dots ( • ), colons inside labels ( Type: ), and trailing ellipses ( ... ) are strictly eliminated. Readable Type Hierarchy : Minimum 14px for metadata, 16px to 18px for body prose, and 28px to 48px for headings. Microscopic 10px text is banned. 3. Comprehensive 5-Dimension Comparison Table Here is how unharnessed models compare directly against an agent governed by the Anti-Slop AI Harness: Operational Dimension ❌ Standard Unharnessed AI ✅ With Anti-Slop AI Harness Response to User Critique Guesses from static pre-training weights; slaps on makeshift labels or generic CSS fixes. Mandatory Live Multi-Archetype Benchmark : Surveys 2 to 3 live industry references (Apple HIG, Stripe, Linear, Pentagram) before touching code. When Given Flawed Prescriptions Sycophantic Yes-Man : Compliments your idea ( "Great point!" ) and implements the destructive patch, degrading the product. 3-Mode Pushback Firewall : Validates your symptom, explains the structural side effect, and delivers a superior Option B . Recurring Error Handling Apologizes repeatedly ( "I apologize for the confusion!" ) and repeats the same bug ten minutes later. 3x Graduation Law : On the 3rd recurrence of any bug pattern, writes an automated linter ( exit code 1 ) to eliminate the bug permanently. Writing & Documentation Robotic AI Slop : Floods text with delve, tapestry, testament, passive hedging, and endless em-dashes. 5-Layer Editorial Engine : Active verbs, Topic-Comment syntax, 15 to 28 word sentence ceiling, zero em-dashes, and strict cliché bans. UI & Visual Layout Sci-Fi Greebling : Clutters views with // , #REF-01 , nested bordered boxes, neon glows, and unreadable 10px fonts. Quiet Luxury Minimalism : Enforces >= 70% Open Canvas , generous whitespace, clean glass badges, and zero fake technical symbols. 4. Real-World Code Examples: Before vs. After To understand the difference this harness makes in practice, examine three concrete transformations across UI styling, behavioral pushback, and technical copy. Example 1: UI Component Refactor (From Greebled Clutter to Quiet Luxury) ❌ Before (Default AI Output with Sci-Fi Greebling) // Typical unharnessed AI response when asked for a "modern telemetry card" export function MetricCard ({ title , value , status }: MetricProps ) { return ( < div className = "border border-cyan-500/40 bg-slate-950 p-4 rounded-lg shadow-cyan-500/20 shadow-lg" > < div className = "flex justify-between items-center text-[10px] text-cyan-400 font-mono tracking-widest border-b border-cyan-800 pb-1 mb-2" > < span > // SYS.REF-049 // span > < span > • STATUS: { status . toUpperCase () } • span > div > < div className = "border border-slate-800 bg-slate-900/60 p-3 rounded mb-2" > < span className = "text-xs text-slate-400 uppercase tracking-wider" > { title } : span > < h3 className = "text-2xl font-bold text-white font-mono" > { value } h3 > div > < p className = "text-[11px] text-slate-500 italic" > CALIBRATION · OK · 2026 p > div > ); } ✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 04 Applied) // Governed by Module 04: >= 70% Open Canvas, Zero Greebling, Clean Glass Card export function MetricCard ({ title , value , status }: MetricProps ) { return ( < div className = "relative rounded-xl border-b-[3px] border-amber-500/80 bg-zinc-900/40 p-6 backdrop-blur-md transition-all hover:bg-zinc-900/60" > < div className = "flex items-baseline justify-between mb-3" > < span className = "text-sm font-medium text-zinc-400" > { title } span > < span className = "text-xs font-medium text-amber-400/90" > { status } span > div > < div className = "text-3xl font-semibold tracking-tight text-zinc-100" > { value } div > div > ); } Notice the immediate difference: the fake slashes, nested boxes, status dots, and illegible ten-pixel font sizes vanish. In their place is a single-layer container with generous padding, clear typographic contrast, and a quiet three-pixel accent bar. Example 2: Behavioral Pushback (From Sycophancy to Principal Architect) Suppose you tell your AI: "The landing page hero looks empty. Add three bordered highlight boxes and a bright red countdown timer in the header." ❌ Before (Unharnessed AI Response) "Great idea! Adding three highlight boxes and a bright red countdown timer will create urgency and make the hero section look much more engaging. I've updated the code with animated red borders and badge components." ✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 02 Pushback Protocol) [HARD-STOP PUSHBACK] 1. Validating the Symptom : You noticed that the top of the page lacks visual tension and doesn't immediately pull the reader into the value proposition. That observation is accurate. 2. Structural Risk : Adding three bordered boxes and a bright red timer will crowd the viewport below the 70% open canvas threshold. On mobile screens, it pushes the primary call-to-action completely below the fold and introduces visual anxiety that cheapens the brand. 3. Option B (World-Class Alternative) : Instead of adding bordered containers and timer clutter, we can: Increase the primary headline font weight from 500 to 700 and tighten line height to 1.05. Introduce an understated editorial kicker badge in muted amber. Add 32px of vertical whitespace above the primary action button. This creates crisp visual punch while keeping the canvas open and calm. If you still want the three boxes, reply override and I will implement them cleanly in an isolated component. Example 3: Technical Product Copy (From AI Buzzwords to Direct Human Prose) ❌ Before (Default AI Slop Copywriting) "In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, our cutting-edge platform allows teams to delve into advanced workflows. It stands as a testament to seamless synergy, empowering builders to unlock their full potential while navigating the complexities of modern software development." ✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 03 Applied) "Most developer tools force you to trade speed for control. We built our pipeline around two commands that run in under five seconds, leaving your existing repository untouched." 5. 30-Second Quickstart Guide (Zero Coding Required) The harness is engineered to install into any modern AI environment without configuration overhead. 1. Cursor IDE Copy the .cursor/ directory from the repository into your project root: your-project/ ├── .cursor/ │ └── rules/ │ ├── 01-benchmark-first-protocol.mdc │ ├── 02-hard-stop-pushback-firewall.mdc │ ├── 03-anti-slop-editorial-voice.mdc │ └── 04-quiet-luxury-ui-anti-greebling.mdc Cursor automatically reads .mdc files and enforces them on every prompt generation. 2. Claude Code CLI & Claude Desktop For Claude Code CLI : Place CLAUDE.md and the .claude/skills/ directory into your project root. For Claude Desktop & Web Projects : Upload the markdown files in rules/ directly into your Project Knowledge or paste them into your Project Instructions. 3. Google Antigravity Global Deployment : Copy GEMINI.md into your global configuration directory at ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md . Project-Level Deployment : Place GEMINI.md and .agents/skills/ into your project repository. 4. ChatGPT (Custom Instructions & Projects) Open your ChatGPT Project settings and paste the unified rules from CLAUDE.md into the Project Instructions. 6. The Funnel Bridge: Free Starter Pack vs. Pro Full Harness Quality AI tooling should not be gatekept behind enterprise sales calls. The Anti-Slop AI Harness is structured across two clean tiers: Tier 1: Free Starter Pack ($0+ on Gumroad / MIT on GitHub) Included : Module 01 ( 01-benchmark-first-protocol ). Formats : Raw .md , Cursor .mdc , Claude/Antigravity SKILL.md , and CLAUDE.md . License : 100% Free and Open Source under the MIT License. GitHub Repository : https://github.com/nguyenlong5238-art/anti-slop-ai-harness Tier 2: Pro Full Harness ($19 Commercial License) Included : All four modules (01 Benchmark Protocol, 02 Pushback Firewall, 03 Editorial Voice Engine, 04 Quiet Luxury UI). Automation Assets : Pre-configured linter graduation templates and CI stop-hook scripts. Bilingual Editions : Complete unabridged specifications in both English and natural Vietnamese. Commercial License : Unlimited use in personal, freelance, and commercial client production projects. Gumroad Storefront : https://longwave04.gumroad.com/l/anti-slop-ai-harness 7. Summary and Next Steps Vibe coding represents the most exciting practical shift in software development in over a decade. But without structural constraints, unharnessed models turn ambitious projects into unmaintainable, slop-ridden prototypes. Give your AI tools the discipline they need. Clone the free MIT repository or install the complete Pro bundle, restart your editor, and experience what happens when your AI assistant thinks like a principal architect. GitHub Repository (Free MIT Starter) : https://github.com/nguyenlong5238-art/anti-slop-ai-harness Gumroad Pro Bundle ($19 Full Harness) : https://longwave04.gumroad.com/l/anti-slop-ai-harness Built by Longwave AI Lab : Autonomous systems, deterministic tooling, and clean editorial craft.

  • Zero Box-in-Box Nesting: Never nest a bordered card inside another bordered card. Visual grouping must use vertical whitespace (16px to 28px), typographic contrast, or a single hairline border (1px at 15% opacity).
  • Punctuation-Free Glass Cards: Visual badges use rounded corners, clean padding, and a single 3px bottom accent bar. Status dots (•), colons inside labels (Type:), and trailing ellipses (...) are strictly eliminated.
  • Readable Type Hierarchy: Minimum 14px for metadata, 16px to 18px for body prose, and 28px to 48px for headings. Microscopic 10px text is banned.
3. Comprehensive 5-Dimension Comparison Table

Here is how unharnessed models compare directly against an agent governed by the Anti-Slop AI Harness:

Operational Dimension ❌ Standard Unharnessed AI ✅ With Anti-Slop AI Harness Response to User Critique Guesses from static pre-training weights; slaps on makeshift labels or generic CSS fixes. Mandatory Live Multi-Archetype Benchmark: Surveys 2 to 3 live industry references (Apple HIG, Stripe, Linear, Pentagram) before touching code. When Given Flawed Prescriptions Sycophantic Yes-Man: Compliments your idea ("Great point!") and implements the destructive patch, degrading the product. 3-Mode Pushback Firewall: Validates your symptom, explains the structural side effect, and delivers a superior Option B. Recurring Error Handling Apologizes repeatedly ("I apologize for the confusion!") and repeats the same bug ten minutes later. 3x Graduation Law: On the 3rd recurrence of any bug pattern, writes an automated linter (exit code 1) to eliminate the bug permanently. Writing & Documentation Robotic AI Slop: Floods text with delve, tapestry, testament, passive hedging, and endless em-dashes. 5-Layer Editorial Engine: Active verbs, Topic-Comment syntax, 15 to 28 word sentence ceiling, zero em-dashes, and strict cliché bans. UI & Visual Layout Sci-Fi Greebling: Clutters views with //, #REF-01, nested bordered boxes, neon glows, and unreadable 10px fonts. Quiet Luxury Minimalism: Enforces >= 70% Open Canvas, generous whitespace, clean glass badges, and zero fake technical symbols.
4. Real-World Code Examples: Before vs. After

To understand the difference this harness makes in practice, examine three concrete transformations across UI styling, behavioral pushback, and technical copy.

Example 1: UI Component Refactor (From Greebled Clutter to Quiet Luxury) ❌ Before (Default AI Output with Sci-Fi Greebling) 
// Typical unharnessed AI response when asked for a "modern telemetry card"
export function MetricCard({ title, value, status }: MetricProps) {
  return (
    <div className="border border-cyan-500/40 bg-slate-950 p-4 rounded-lg shadow-cyan-500/20 shadow-lg">
      <div className="flex justify-between items-center text-[10px] text-cyan-400 font-mono tracking-widest border-b border-cyan-800 pb-1 mb-2">
        <span>// SYS.REF-049 //span>
        <span>• STATUS: {status.toUpperCase()} •span>
      div>
      <div className="border border-slate-800 bg-slate-900/60 p-3 rounded mb-2">
        <span className="text-xs text-slate-400 uppercase tracking-wider">{title}:span>
        <h3 className="text-2xl font-bold text-white font-mono">{value}h3>
      div>
      <p className="text-[11px] text-slate-500 italic">CALIBRATION · OK · 2026p>
    div>
  );
}
✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 04 Applied) 
// Governed by Module 04: >= 70% Open Canvas, Zero Greebling, Clean Glass Card
export function MetricCard({ title, value, status }: MetricProps) {
  return (
    <div className="relative rounded-xl border-b-[3px] border-amber-500/80 bg-zinc-900/40 p-6 backdrop-blur-md transition-all hover:bg-zinc-900/60">
      <div className="flex items-baseline justify-between mb-3">
        <span className="text-sm font-medium text-zinc-400">{title}span>
        <span className="text-xs font-medium text-amber-400/90">{status}span>
      div>
      <div className="text-3xl font-semibold tracking-tight text-zinc-100">
        {value}
      div>

}

Notice the immediate difference: the fake slashes, nested boxes, status dots, and illegible ten-pixel font sizes vanish. In their place is a single-layer container with generous padding, clear typographic contrast, and a quiet three-pixel accent bar.

Example 2: Behavioral Pushback (From Sycophancy to Principal Architect)

Suppose you tell your AI: "The landing page hero looks empty. Add three bordered highlight boxes and a bright red countdown timer in the header."

❌ Before (Unharnessed AI Response)

✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 02 Pushback Protocol)

[HARD-STOP PUSHBACK]

1. Validating the Symptom: You noticed that the top of the page lacks visual tension and doesn't immediately pull the reader into the value proposition. That observation is accurate.

2. Structural Risk: Adding three bordered boxes and a bright red timer will crowd the viewport below the 70% open canvas threshold. On mobile screens, it pushes the primary call-to-action completely below the fold and introduces visual anxiety that cheapens the brand.

3. Option B (World-Class Alternative): Instead of adding bordered containers and timer clutter, we can:

  • Increase the primary headline font weight from 500 to 700 and tighten line height to 1.05.
  • Introduce an understated editorial kicker badge in muted amber.
  • Add 32px of vertical whitespace above the primary action button.

This creates crisp visual punch while keeping the canvas open and calm. If you still want the three boxes, reply override and I will implement them cleanly in an isolated component.

items.title: Perplexity and NVIDIA Researchers Introduce JOLT: a Joint Teacher-Student Reinforcement Learning Method
items.summary: Perplexity , along with NVIDIA team, has introduced JOLT, a new post-training method for language models. JOLT stands for Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching . It trains a single model in 2 roles. The teacher sees privileged information; the student does not. The key change is that the teacher is trained too, so its feedback stays usable. On MATH, JOLT matched GRPO’s accuracy with 6.5x fewer processed training tokens. For teams running RL post-training, that is a direct compute question. TL;DR What it is: a post-training method. Size: tested on Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Runs on: 1 shared model plays both roles, so no separate teacher model. Training hardware: Not disclosed. Performance: JOLT+ posts the highest mean score in every setting tested against GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill. Best: AppWorld state-test pass rate of 72.09% with JOLT+, vs 62.20% for GRPO (+9.9 points). Worst: JOLT without student reward scores 51.92% on AppWorld, below GRPO. What is Perplexity JOLT? JOLT is a self-distillation method from Perplexity and NVIDIA that trains one model as teacher and student. It builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) . Why does RL post-training need a better teacher? Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO , gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow. On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution. The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training. How does JOLT work? JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time: Teacher: gets privileged information. It learns from outcome rewards, plus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the student. Student: sees only the task. It learns from the teacher’s token-level distillation signal on its own attempts. On-policy: each role learns from trajectories generated under its own context. JOLT+: adds the student’s own outcome reward to the student update. The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy. && How does JOLT perform on benchmarks? The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information: GSM8K: DeepSeek-V2-Lite; teacher gets the verified answer. MATH: Qwen3-0.6B; teacher gets worked reference solutions. LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen3-8B on 131 problems; teacher gets a passing sibling solution or execution feedback. AppWorld: Qwen3-4B-Instruct; teacher gets summaries of past attempts. Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct trained on TMax ; teacher gets private verifier files. JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 , JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%. Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%. How much training compute does JOLT save? On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens. JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD. How does JOLT compare with GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill? All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper , with hyperparameters tuned per method. Method descriptions link to each method’s own paper. Feature JOLT JOLT+ GRPO OPSD π-Distill Separate teacher model No No No teacher No (self-teacher) No (shared model) Teacher is trained Yes (reward + KL to student) Yes (reward + KL to student) Not applicable No Yes (KL-regularized) Student signal Dense distillation, on-policy Distillation + outcome reward Group-relative outcome reward Dense distillation, on-policy Off-policy, teacher trajectories MATH, Qwen3-0.6B (%) 72.14 ± 0.90 72.59 ± 1.17 68.36 ± 3.73 61.20 ± 2.10 42.25 ± 1.10 LCBv6, Qwen3-8B (%) 47.64 ± 1.10 49.08 ± 0.41 46.13 ± 1.83 45.34 ± 1.50 38.23 ± 1.72 AppWorld, Qwen3-4B (%) 51.92 ± 5.30 72.09 ± 6.01 62.20 ± 2.83 29.49 ± 2.48 59.85 ± 2.97 Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 (%) 6.56 10.96 8.25 2.82 4.99 Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@32 (%) 25.69 34.83 30.34 16.90 22.31 Code Not yet released Not yet released Not disclosed GitHub Not disclosed Terminal-Bench base model: 5.18% pass@1, 22.81% pass@32. Key Takeaways 1 model plays teacher and student, and the teacher is trained too. 6.5x fewer processed tokens than GRPO at matched MATH accuracy. JOLT+ beats GRPO by 9.9 points on AppWorld. Plain JOLT still trails GRPO on AppWorld and Terminal-Bench. Check out the paper on arXiv and the Perplexity research blog post . All credit goes to the researcher of this project.
