items.summary_html:
Perplexity, along with NVIDIA team, has introduced JOLT, a new post-training method for language models. JOLT stands for Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching. It trains a single model in 2 roles. The teacher sees privileged information; the student does not. The key change is that the teacher is trained too, so its feedback stays usable. On MATH, JOLT matched GRPO’s accuracy with 6.5x fewer processed training tokens. For teams running RL post-training, that is a direct compute question.

TL;DR
  • What it is: a post-training method.
  • Size: tested on Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite.
  • Runs on: 1 shared model plays both roles, so no separate teacher model. Training hardware: Not disclosed.
  • Performance: JOLT+ posts the highest mean score in every setting tested against GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill.
  • Best: AppWorld state-test pass rate of 72.09% with JOLT+, vs 62.20% for GRPO (+9.9 points).
  • Worst: JOLT without student reward scores 51.92% on AppWorld, below GRPO.
What is Perplexity JOLT?

JOLT is a self-distillation method from Perplexity and NVIDIA that trains one model as teacher and student. It builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD).

Why does RL post-training need a better teacher?

Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO, gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow.

On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution.

The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training.

How does JOLT work?

JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time:

  • Teacher: gets privileged information. It learns from outcome rewards, plus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the student.
  • Student: sees only the task. It learns from the teacher’s token-level distillation signal on its own attempts.
  • On-policy: each role learns from trajectories generated under its own context.
  • JOLT+: adds the student’s own outcome reward to the student update.

The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy.

&&

How does JOLT perform on benchmarks?

The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information:

  • GSM8K: DeepSeek-V2-Lite; teacher gets the verified answer.
  • MATH: Qwen3-0.6B; teacher gets worked reference solutions.
  • LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen3-8B on 131 problems; teacher gets a passing sibling solution or execution feedback.
  • AppWorld: Qwen3-4B-Instruct; teacher gets summaries of past attempts.
  • Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct trained on TMax; teacher gets private verifier files.

JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%.

Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%.

How much training compute does JOLT save?

On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens.

JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD.

How does JOLT compare with GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill?

All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper, with hyperparameters tuned per method. Method descriptions link to each method’s own paper.

FeatureJOLTJOLT+GRPOOPSDπ-DistillSeparate teacher modelNoNoNo teacherNo (self-teacher)No (shared model)Teacher is trainedYes (reward + KL to student)Yes (reward + KL to student)Not applicableNoYes (KL-regularized)Student signalDense distillation, on-policyDistillation + outcome rewardGroup-relative outcome rewardDense distillation, on-policyOff-policy, teacher trajectoriesMATH, Qwen3-0.6B (%)72.14 ± 0.9072.59 ± 1.1768.36 ± 3.7361.20 ± 2.1042.25 ± 1.10LCBv6, Qwen3-8B (%)47.64 ± 1.1049.08 ± 0.4146.13 ± 1.8345.34 ± 1.5038.23 ± 1.72AppWorld, Qwen3-4B (%)51.92 ± 5.3072.09 ± 6.0162.20 ± 2.8329.49 ± 2.4859.85 ± 2.97Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 (%)6.5610.968.252.824.99Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@32 (%)25.6934.8330.3416.9022.31CodeNot yet releasedNot yet releasedNot disclosedGitHubNot disclosed

Terminal-Bench base model: 5.18% pass@1, 22.81% pass@32.

Key Takeaways
  • 1 model plays teacher and student, and the teacher is trained too.
  • 6.5x fewer processed tokens than GRPO at matched MATH accuracy.
  • JOLT+ beats GRPO by 9.9 points on AppWorld.
  • Plain JOLT still trails GRPO on AppWorld and Terminal-Bench.

Check out the paper on arXiv and the Perplexity research blog post. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: PHP2Shell: How AI Found a 14-Year-Old Bug in PHP, and Why the Patch Race Is On
items.summary: Two critical flaws in the engine behind a huge share of the web, an early leak, and a preview of how AI changes security work for both defenders and attackers. The short version On October 21, PHP shipped emergency updates for two critical flaws, CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and let an attacker with no account run code on a web server. OpenAI says the underlying bug had been sitting in PHP for 14 years. What makes this story different is who found it: AI-assisted researchers, before attackers did, as far as anyone knows. thehackernews Fortune How AI found it Security firm Calif found the first flaw in August with help from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Calif had been invited to OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which proactively hunts for flaws in digital infrastructure. Google-owned Wiz found the flaws independently, weeks later. Wiz says it used its own Wiz Atlas tool plus Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to adapt exploits across PHP versions and setups. PHP rushes out emergency patches for two critical bugs AI found first +3 Note what “AI found it” means here. Humans steered, and the models did heavy lifting on discovery and exploit development. Calif itself cautions that no model can unearth all bugs from simple prompts. The Hacker News also reports that knowing the target’s history still mattered. cyberkendra thehackernews OpenAI says frontier AI found these flaws before attackers did, giving maintainers a “Defender’s Window” to prepare fixes and protections. The result was a two-month effort between OpenAI, PHP maintainers, researchers and security providers. cyberscoopcyberscoop How attackers can abuse it Here is the concept in plain terms, at the level the public advisories describe it. Both flaws are use-after-free bugs. A fatal error mid-request, typically running out of memory, interrupts PHP before it cleans up, and a later request or reused worker then treats the freed memory as live data. Every known trigger is a multipart/form-data request, the format used for file uploads, and PHP parses it before your application code runs. That is why no login is needed and why your own code quality doesn’t matter. sansecsansec Two outcomes matter. One flaw can leak memory on its own, similar to Heartbleed, exposing passwords, session tokens, API keys and TLS private keys from other requests. The other leads to remote code execution, and an exploit tool credited to Calif combines both bugs into one attack that needs no login. Calif demonstrated it against WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel and other popular PHP apps. After a break-in, defenders are told to look for web shells, new files in the web root, cron jobs, scheduled tasks and new accounts. PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (CVE-2026–109618, CVE-2026–109619) +3 How it unfolded The disclosure was meant to be orderly. Details leaked on October 20, PHP pulled its release forward a day, and Calif had mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept. Chainguard also published patched images about six hours before the official fix. thehackernews Is it being exploited? Attempts, yes. Confirmed breaches, not yet reported. Cloudflare saw attack traffic and watched attackers change payloads to get around its firewall rules, and watchTowr confirmed active exploitation attempts against both flaws. No source had reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server at the time of the update. Some organizations went offline as a precaution, including BambooHR and several Dutch government sites. Sansec expects mass exploitation now that the patch and write-ups are public. PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge +2 What to do Update the PHP runtime, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM and long-running workers. Fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. thehackernews Updating WordPress or Laravel does not update PHP. It comes from your server package, host or container image. thehackernews Config workarounds only reduce specific attack paths. Updating is the only complete fix. thehackernews PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates, though source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. thehackernews The bigger picture Wiz compares PHP2Shell to Heartbleed, and coverage puts its potential reach at around 70% of the internet. Treat that as a headline estimate, not a measured figure. The lasting lesson is the economics. Wiz says AI turned a long-standing flaw into a practical exploit. OpenAI expects similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Old bugs that were “too hard to exploit” are getting cheaper to prove, for defenders and attackers alike. The advantage goes to whoever patches fastest. PHP2Shell: How AI Found a 14-Year-Old Bug in PHP, and Why the Patch Race Is On was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

The short version

On October 21, PHP shipped emergency updates for two critical flaws, CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and let an attacker with no account run code on a web server. OpenAI says the underlying bug had been sitting in PHP for 14 years. What makes this story different is who found it: AI-assisted researchers, before attackers did, as far as anyone knows. thehackernewsFortune

How AI found it

Security firm Calif found the first flaw in August with help from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Calif had been invited to OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which proactively hunts for flaws in digital infrastructure. Google-owned Wiz found the flaws independently, weeks later. Wiz says it used its own Wiz Atlas tool plus Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to adapt exploits across PHP versions and setups. PHP rushes out emergency patches for two critical bugs AI found first +3

Note what “AI found it” means here. Humans steered, and the models did heavy lifting on discovery and exploit development. Calif itself cautions that no model can unearth all bugs from simple prompts. The Hacker News also reports that knowing the target’s history still mattered. cyberkendrathehackernews

OpenAI says frontier AI found these flaws before attackers did, giving maintainers a “Defender’s Window” to prepare fixes and protections. The result was a two-month effort between OpenAI, PHP maintainers, researchers and security providers. cyberscoopcyberscoop

How attackers can abuse it

Here is the concept in plain terms, at the level the public advisories describe it. Both flaws are use-after-free bugs. A fatal error mid-request, typically running out of memory, interrupts PHP before it cleans up, and a later request or reused worker then treats the freed memory as live data. Every known trigger is a multipart/form-data request, the format used for file uploads, and PHP parses it before your application code runs. That is why no login is needed and why your own code quality doesn’t matter. sansecsansec

Two outcomes matter. One flaw can leak memory on its own, similar to Heartbleed, exposing passwords, session tokens, API keys and TLS private keys from other requests. The other leads to remote code execution, and an exploit tool credited to Calif combines both bugs into one attack that needs no login. Calif demonstrated it against WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel and other popular PHP apps. After a break-in, defenders are told to look for web shells, new files in the web root, cron jobs, scheduled tasks and new accounts. PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (CVE-2026–109618, CVE-2026–109619) +3

How it unfolded

The disclosure was meant to be orderly. Details leaked on October 20, PHP pulled its release forward a day, and Calif had mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept. Chainguard also published patched images about six hours before the official fix. thehackernews

Is it being exploited?

Attempts, yes. Confirmed breaches, not yet reported. Cloudflare saw attack traffic and watched attackers change payloads to get around its firewall rules, and watchTowr confirmed active exploitation attempts against both flaws. No source had reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server at the time of the update. Some organizations went offline as a precaution, including BambooHR and several Dutch government sites. Sansec expects mass exploitation now that the patch and write-ups are public. PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge +2

What to do

  • Update the PHP runtime, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM and long-running workers. Fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. thehackernews
  • Updating WordPress or Laravel does not update PHP. It comes from your server package, host or container image. thehackernews
  • Config workarounds only reduce specific attack paths. Updating is the only complete fix. thehackernews
  • PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates, though source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. thehackernews

The bigger picture

Wiz compares PHP2Shell to Heartbleed, and coverage puts its potential reach at around 70% of the internet. Treat that as a headline estimate, not a measured figure. The lasting lesson is the economics. Wiz says AI turned a long-standing flaw into a practical exploit. OpenAI expects similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Old bugs that were “too hard to exploit” are getting cheaper to prove, for defenders and attackers alike. The advantage goes to whoever patches fastest.

PHP2Shell: How AI Found a 14-Year-Old Bug in PHP, and Why the Patch Race Is On was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.summary_html:
Cost-Effective Multimodal AI- Deploy Vision GGUF Models with Llama.cpp on SageMaker

The “Local LLM” revolution has given us incredible tools like llama.cpp and the GGUF format, allowing us to run high-performance Vision models on modest hardware. But there is a massive leap between running an OCR model in a local terminal and serving it as a production-grade, auto-scaling API on the cloud.

When you need to move beyond “it works on my machine,” Amazon SageMaker is the gold standard. However, SageMaker’s pre-built environments don’t always support the cutting-edge efficiency of quantized GGUF vision models.

To bridge this gap, we must go BYOC (Bring Your Own Container).

By wrapping the raw speed of llama.cpp inside the modern, asynchronous architecture of FastAPI, we can create a custom inference engine that SageMaker treats like any other managed endpoint. This approach gives you the best of both worlds: the extreme memory efficiency of 4-bit quantization and the industrial-strength reliability of AWS.

In this end-to-end guide, we will build a custom OCR solution that handles complex visual reasoning without the “GPU tax” of unquantized models. We’ll cover:

  • Building a SageMaker-compatible Docker container from scratch.
  • Architecting a FastAPI wrapper to handle the /invocations and /ping lifecycle.
  • Optimizing Vision-Language GGUF models for high-speed text extraction.
  • Deploying the final stack to a live SageMaker Endpoint.
  1. Prerequisites and Setup

First, verify Docker is running and install the Hugging Face Hub library to pull our model weights.

!docker version
!pip install huggingface-hub

We’ll dynamically pull your AWS account details to ensure this script is portable across regions.

Note: Ensure you replace "your-bucket-name"with an actual S3 bucket in your account.
import subprocess
S3_BUCKET_NAME = "bucket_name" # Please change the Bucketname when you running this cell
ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME = "ecr_repo_name"
AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = subprocess.check_output("aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text", shell=True).decode().strip()
AWS_REGION = subprocess.check_output("aws configure get region", shell=True).decode().strip()
ECR_URI=f"{AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}.dkr.ecr.{AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com"
ECR_REPOSITORY_URI=f"{ECR_URI}/{ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME}"
IMAGE_TAG="latest"
MODEL_NAME="Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf"

2. Downloading GGUF Model Files

We need two files: the quantized weights and the multimodal projector (the “eyes” of the model). We’ll use the Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF, which is highly efficient for document text extraction.

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import os

GGUF_NAME = "Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf"
MM_PROJ_NAME = "mmproj-F16.gguf"

MODEL_PATH = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="unsloth/Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF",
    filename=GGUF_NAME,
    local_dir="~/SageMaker/workspace/",
    local_dir_use_symlinks=False
)

MMPROJ_PATH = hf_hub_download(
    repo_id="unsloth/Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF",
    filename=MMPROJ_NAME,
    local_dir=r"/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/workspace",
    local_dir_use_symlinks=False,
)

print("✅ Model:", MODEL_PATH)
print("📦 Size:", round(os.path.getsize(MODEL_PATH)/1024/1024, 2), "MB")

3. Implementing the FastAPI Inference Server

Our main.py handles the SageMaker lifecycle. We use Lazy Loading for the model to ensure the container starts quickly, though the very first request will bear the "Cold Start" load time.

%%writefile main.py
import os, base64, io, logging
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response
from PIL import Image, ImageOps, ImageEnhance
from llama_cpp import Llama
from llama_cpp.llama_chat_format import MiniCPMv26ChatHandler

# Setup logging to see output in SageMaker/Docker logs
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

app = FastAPI()

# --- DIAGNOSTIC LOGGING BLOCK ---
MODEL_DIR = "/opt/ml/model"
logger.info(f"Checking directory: {MODEL_DIR}")

if os.path.exists(MODEL_DIR):
    # List all files and subdirectories found in the model path
    contents = []
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(MODEL_DIR):
        for name in files:
            contents.append(os.path.join(root, name))
    
    if contents:
        logger.info(f"✅ FOUND {len(contents)} files in {MODEL_DIR}:")
        for f in contents:
            # Print file size to ensure it's not a 0-byte corrupted download
            size_mb = os.path.getsize(f) / (1024 * 1024)
            logger.info(f" - {f} ({size_mb:.2f} MB)")
    else:
        logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} exists but is EMPTY.")
else:
    logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} directory DOES NOT EXIST.")

# SageMaker unpacks S3 model.tar.gz into /opt/ml/model
MODEL_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf"
MMPROJ_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/mmproj-F16.gguf"

# Global model variable for lazy loading
llm = None

def load_model():
    global llm
    if llm is None:
        chat_handler = MiniCPMv26ChatHandler(clip_model_path=MMPROJ_PATH, verbose=False)
        llm = Llama(
            model_path=MODEL_PATH,
            chat_handler=chat_handler,
            n_ctx=2096, #max for t4 is 128000 (128k) , we have limited to 2096 (2k context)
            n_gpu_layers=-1, 
            verbose=False
        )

@app.get("/ping")
async def ping():
    return Response(status_code=200)

@app.post("/invocations")
async def invocations(request: Request):
    load_model() 
    
    payload = await request.json()
    
    # 1. Standardize input to a list of tasks
    # This supports {"image": "..."} OR {"images": ["...", "..."]}
    raw_images = payload.get("images", [])
    if not raw_images and "image" in payload:
        raw_images = [payload["image"]]
        
    prompt = payload.get("prompt", "Extract all text from this image")
    max_tokens = int(payload.get("max_tokens", 512))
    temperature = float(payload.get("temperature", 0.0))
    
    if not raw_images:
        return Response(content="Missing 'image' or 'images' in payload", status_code=400)

    results = []

    # 2. Process the batch sequentially
    for i, image_b64 in enumerate(raw_images):
        try:
            out = llm.create_chat_completion(
                messages=[{
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": [
                        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{image_b64}"}},
                        {"type": "text", "text": prompt},
                    ],
                }],
                max_tokens=max_tokens,
                temperature=temperature,
            )
            
            results.append({
                "index": i,
                "text": out["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip(),
                "finish_reason": out["choices"][0].get("finish_reason"),
                "usage": out.get("usage")
            })
        except Exception as e:
            results.append({"index": i, "error": str(e)})
    
    # 3. Return the batch result
    return {"results": results}

4. Building the Docker Image (BYOC)

We use a multi-stage build to keep the runtime image lean. We pull a pre-compiled llama-cpp-python wheel for CUDA 12.4 to avoid lengthy compilation times during the build.

%%writefile Dockerfile
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 AS builder
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3-pip python3-dev
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip
RUN pip install llama-cpp-python --extra-index-url https://abetlen.github.io/llama-cpp-python/whl/cu124
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir fastapi uvicorn pillow

FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/bin /usr/local/bin
COPY main.py .
RUN mkdir -p /opt/ml/model
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

5. Packaging and Pushing

Crucial Step: When creating the model.tar.gz, ensure the files are at the root of the archive so SageMaker finds them at /opt/ml/model/.

# Package artifacts
!tar -cvzf model.tar.gz Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf mmproj-F16.gguf

# Upload to S3
!aws s3 cp model.tar.gz s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz

# Build and Push Container
!aws ecr get-login-password --region {AWS_REGION} | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin {ECR_URI}
!docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" .
!docker tag "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"
!docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"Upload to S3 bucket

Building and pushing image to ECR

!docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG" .
!docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"

6. Deployment to SageMaker Endpoint

We deploy to an ml.g4dn.xlarge instance. Even though GGUF is efficient on CPUs, using the NVIDIA T4 GPU ensures low-latency OCR performance.

import sagemaker
from sagemaker.model import Model

role = sagemaker.get_execution_role()
container_uri = f"{ECR_REPOSITORY_URI}:{IMAGE_TAG}"
model_s3_url = f"s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz"

ocr_model = Model(
    image_uri=container_uri,
    model_data=model_s3_url,
    role=role,
    name="nanonets-ocr-gguf-model"
)

predictor = ocr_model.deploy(
    initial_instance_count=1,
    instance_type="ml.g4dn.xlarge",
    endpoint_name="vision-ocr-endpoint",
    container_startup_health_check_timeout=600
)

7. Conclusion

By combining llama.cpp and SageMaker BYOC, you’ve built a production-grade OCR pipeline that is both high-performance and cost-aware. You are no longer restricted by pre-built cloud containers and can leverage the latest quantized multimodal models as soon as they drop on Hugging Face.

Don’t forget to clean up:

sagemaker_c = boto3.client('sagemaker')
sagemaker_c.delete_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name)
sagemaker_c.get_waiter('endpoint_deleted').wait(EndpointName=endpoint_name)
print("Endpoint + model deleted!")

Deploying Vision GGUF Models to Amazon SageMaker with llama.cpp was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Is Cursor Becoming a Grok-First Editor?
items.summary: Models from different labs are part of Cursor’s appeal. Its new plans change which of them your subscription actually pays for. Illustration generated with AI. What appeals to me about Cursor is the ability to use models from different labs in one editor. You can choose the model that works best for a particular task, rather than expect one model to be the best at everything. Cursor’s supported models That choice matters over time, too. A month later, a new release may change which model you prefer. I want to be able to use it without having to rethink my whole setup. Committing my workflow to one lab would mean giving up part of the reason for using a multi-model tool. That is what interests me about Cursor’s new plans. How much of that flexibility are you still paying for? What changes if you use models from several labs? The useful comparison is with what a Cursor subscriber already gets. Legacy Pro, Pro+ and Ultra plans include an allowance for third-party models through an “Other Models” pool. Switching to The X Subscription removes that allowance. Existing subscribers can keep their old plan, price and features, so this is a decision to evaluate before switching. Cursor’s legacy-plan comparison The new bundle was announced on October 12 and includes Cursor, Grok and X benefits. The X Subscription announcement On the new individual Premium plan, $30 a month before tax includes usage for Grok and Composer. If you directly select Claude, GPT or Gemini, you pay for that usage separately at API list price using prepaid credit. Super and Ultra work the same way for direct third-party model selection. The $8 Plus plan does not offer third-party models. Current individual plans The included model pool lists both Grok and Composer. Source: Cursor documentation , captured October 19, 2026. items.title: Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story
items.summary: For two decades, data centres were relatively safe, lucrative real estate investments. They attracted investors because they served as digital infrastructure — the essential plumbing that keeps the internet running. The growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and its increased demands on computing power has meant data centre builders are in a race to build out sufficient supply. But in the past two weeks, investors have started to have genuine concerns about the long-term viability of these businesses. On Wednesday, shares in NextDC, one of Australia’s largest data centre builders, collapsed by 40% after it said delays at its flagship Melbourne site meant its revenue forecasts would fall short of forecasts. These delays have come about after the local community raised significant concerns about the impact of NextDC’s M3 data centre expansion. Electricity distributor Jemena paused the construction of the giant concrete power poles that had been snaking their way along Footscray streets, after local councils raised concerns about the impact on residential neighbourhoods. These 22-metre power poles are crucial to NextDC’s operations in Footscray. Data centre operators make their profits from selling access to the massive amounts of power that AI chips need. Without that power, these facilities cannot remain viable. NextDC is not alone in facing significant headwinds. Data centre company Firmus abruptly cancelled its multi-billion dollar listing on the Australian stock exchange, due to a lack of investor demand. Similarly, London-based data centre developer Nscale is struggling to attract buyers for a stock market listing on Wall Street. Shares in CoreWeave, which claims to operate the world’s most powerful AI supercomputer , dropped 15% in one day last week on concerns about its financial strength. These jitters reflect the harsh reality of AI: while the hype is strong, the business models are coming under increasing scrutiny. Rising costs for massive investments Hundreds of billions of dollars have been spent globally on training models and building the data centres to house the infrastructure that powers AI. The pipeline of investments is expected to reach some US$10 trillion (A$14.25 trillion) by 2032. Until recently, much of the capital expenditure was funded internally by the AI companies or by raising money directly from investors; more recently, they have been borrowing vast sums in the corporate bond market. And while those investing in AI are patient, they still expect to see significant financial returns. Community campaigners demonstrating against a planned data centre in Kilmarnock, Scotland. Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images Sticky inflation and rising interest rates complicate this further. Data centre developers now face higher borrowing costs, plus higher construction costs. And rising interest rates can make other investments more attractive. Analysts estimate that giants like OpenAI and Anthropic will need to increase revenues by 80% a year for the next six years to meet investors’ revenue expectations. Yet, indicators suggest that consumer and corporate spending on paid AI models is slowing down . Racing for chips To make things worse, the hardware that AI depends upon is driving real investor concern. Historically, data centres could operate for decades with minimal maintenance, guaranteeing rents and returns. But AI chips have a shelf life of only a few years. Each new generation requires upgrades to power delivery and cooling, trapping data centres on a treadmill of multibillion-dollar expenses to pay for these upgrades. Even if AI revenues stabilise enough to support these expenses, there’s no guarantee that data centre companies will be able to access the chips they need to fill data centres, and to support AI demand. Amazon recently admitted it is hoarding billions of AI chips, even though it doesn’t have any capacity for installing them . This massive over-investment is driven by anxieties around long-term supplies. This gold rush for chips is why American chip manufacturer Nvidia is one of the few companies in the AI space to actually be making money. Nvidia also invests in the companies that buy its chips — its own customers — raising concerns about circular financing . The social licence Beyond the balance sheet, investors are also concerned about the loss of social licence for data centres amid local community protests. Community concerns around data centres are already high , driven by persistent noise (from energy transmission), visual impact, localised heating, and environmental concerns . And these concerns will only grow if data centres start to impact the cost of living by pushing up electricity or water prices. Forecasts suggest that New South Wales data centres could consume up to 25% of Sydney’s daily water demand within a decade. In Victoria, transmission company AusNet is reviewing requests from data centres for more than 10 gigawatts of connections, which could exceed the state’s entire supply capacity . In both cases, this level of demand will inevitably affect consumer prices. When will communities benefit? The AI age depends on the physical infrastructure of data centres. But the current path we are on demands ever-increasing capital from investors to fund a relentless upgrade cycle. It demands huge volumes of power and water from local utilities. And it places a significant burden on the communities that host these data centres. These factors mean the era of data centres being a safe stock market investment are over. And if investors become unwilling to fund these risks blindly, and communities become resistant to hosting these centres, this month’s stock market jitters may turn into a steeper market sell-off. To shore up investor confidence, it’s important that investments in AI do not just focus on building better models, but also models that are more efficient — in terms of their costs, energy demands and spatial requirements. And if they can be designed to support the electricity grid by adding, rather than displacing, renewables capacity, then communities may begin to feel the benefits of investments into AI.

But in the past two weeks, investors have started to have genuine concerns about the long-term viability of these businesses. Similarly, London-based data centre developer Nscale is struggling to attract buyers for a stock market listing on Wall Street. Shares in CoreWeave, which claims to operate the world’s most powerful AI supercomputer, dropped 15% in one day last week on concerns about its financial strength.

These jitters reflect the harsh reality of AI: while the hype is strong, the business models are coming under increasing scrutiny.

Rising costs for massive investments

Hundreds of billions of dollars have been spent globally on training models and building the data centres to house the infrastructure that powers AI. The pipeline of investments is expected to reach some US$10 trillion (A$14.25 trillion) by 2032.

Until recently, much of the capital expenditure was funded internally by the AI companies or by raising money directly from investors; more recently, they have been borrowing vast sums in the corporate bond market.

Community campaigners demonstrating against a planned data centre in Kilmarnock, Scotland. Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images

Sticky inflation and rising interest rates complicate this further. Data centre developers now face higher borrowing costs, plus higher construction costs. And rising interest rates can make other investments more attractive.

Analysts estimate that giants like OpenAI and Anthropic will need to increase revenues by 80% a year for the next six years to meet investors’ revenue expectations. Yet, indicators suggest that consumer and corporate spending on paid AI models is slowing down.

Racing for chips

To make things worse, the hardware that AI depends upon is driving real investor concern. Historically, data centres could operate for decades with minimal maintenance, guaranteeing rents and returns.

Even if AI revenues stabilise enough to support these expenses, there’s no guarantee that data centre companies will be able to access the chips they need to fill data centres, and to support AI demand. In Victoria, transmission company AusNet is reviewing requests from data centres for more than 10 gigawatts of connections, which could exceed the state’s entire supply capacity.

In both cases, this level of demand will inevitably affect consumer prices.

When will communities benefit?

The AI age depends on the physical infrastructure of data centres. But the current path we are on demands ever-increasing capital from investors to fund a relentless upgrade cycle.

It demands huge volumes of power and water from local utilities. And it places a significant burden on the communities that host these data centres.

And if they can be designed to support the electricity grid by adding, rather than displacing, renewables capacity, then communities may begin to feel the benefits of investments into AI.

items.title: A Coding Guide to Cactus Whistle: Does a 16.9 MB Speech Model Hold Up Against Whisper Base? Word Error Rate, Speed, Streaming, Timestamps, Keywords, and Speech-to-Tool Calls on a CPU
items.summary:
In this tutorial, we use Whistle , Cactus Compute’s speech-to-text model, a 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU, transcribes seven languages, and returns word timestamps and probabilities. The model card claims it beats Whisper base on LibriSpeech; we test it on seeded test-clean and test-other samples, comparing Whistle with Whisper tiny and base on identical clips, judged by paired speaker-cluster intervals with Holm correction. We find a lead over greedy Whisper base on test-other, no significant gap against beam search, and a speed advantage that narrows as clips grow. Beyond the headline, we probe a 30-second window where the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, plus streaming latency, timestamps, keyword biasing, other languages, noise, embeddings, and speech-to-tool calls. Our figures are one-run samples from an Apple M4, and published full-split numbers are quoted, not measured. items.summary_html:
In this tutorial, we use Whistle, Cactus Compute’s speech-to-text model, a 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU, transcribes seven languages, and returns word timestamps and probabilities. The model card claims it beats Whisper base on LibriSpeech; we test it on seeded test-clean and test-other samples, comparing Whistle with Whisper tiny and base on identical clips, judged by paired speaker-cluster intervals with Holm correction. We find a lead over greedy Whisper base on test-other, no significant gap against beam search, and a speed advantage that narrows as clips grow. Beyond the headline, we probe a 30-second window where the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, plus streaming latency, timestamps, keyword biasing, other languages, noise, embeddings, and speech-to-tool calls. Our figures are one-run samples from an Apple M4, and published full-split numbers are quoted, not measured.

def banner(title):

def section(name):
    def wrap(fn):
        def run(*a, **kw):
            banner(name)
            t0 = time.time()
            try:
                out = fn(*a, **kw)
                RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok"
                return out
            except Exception as e:
                RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
                print(f"\n[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                traceback.print_exc(limit=3)
                return None
            finally:
                print(f"\n[{time.time() - t0:.0f} s]")
                json.dump({"results": RESULTS, "verdicts": VERDICTS}, open("results.json", "w"), indent=1)
        return run
    return wrap

def fetch(url, tries=7):
    """GET with retries. The datasets-server rate-limits anonymous callers (HTTP 429): honour Retry-After when it is
    sent, otherwise back off 5, 10, 20, 40 ... seconds, and never give up on the first refusal."""
    for k in range(tries):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as r:
                return r.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if k == tries - 1:
                raise
            wait = int(e.headers.get("Retry-After", 0) or 0) if e.code == 429 else 0
            time.sleep(max(wait, 5 * 2 ** k) if e.code in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) else 2)
        except Exception:
            if k == tries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(3 * (k + 1))
 
 
def page(dataset, config, split, offset, length=100):

    if sr != SR:

    return audio, hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()[:12]

import jiwer
import whisper
import torch
from whisper.normalizers import EnglishTextNormalizer, BasicTextNormalizer
 
NORM_EN = EnglishTextNormalizer()      # the normalisers Whistle's own benchmarks use; applied to both sides, always
NORM_BASIC = BasicTextNormalizer()
SEED = 2026
N_WHISTLE = 300                        # clips per LibriSpeech split that Whistle transcribes (it is cheap)
N_PAIRED = {"other": 100, "clean": 60}  # the first N of them also go through Whisper (it is not); test-other is primary
MAX_CLIP_S = 30.0                      # Whistle's single-pass window; longer clips are declared out of scope here
WHISPER_SECONDS = collections.Counter()
 
 
def all_rows(dataset, config, split):
    out, offset = [], 0
    while True:
        rows = page(dataset, config, split, offset)["rows"]
        out += [r["row"] for r in rows]
        offset += 100
        if len(rows) < 100:
            return out
 
 
def dataset_sha(dataset):
    return json.loads(fetch(f"https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/{dataset}"))["sha"][:12]
 
 
def wer_counts(ref, hyp):
    """Errors (S+D+I) and reference words for one normalised pair; an empty hypothesis is all deletions."""
    n = len(ref.split())
    if not hyp.strip():
        return n, n
    o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp)
    return o.substitutions + o.deletions + o.insertions, n
 
 
def sdi(ref, hyp):
    if not hyp.strip():
        return 0, len(ref.split()), 0
    o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp)
    return o.substitutions, o.deletions, o.insertions
 
 
def corpus_wer(errs, words):
    return 100.0 * sum(errs) / max(sum(words), 1)
 
 
def _by_cluster(clusters, *arrays):
    tot = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0.0] * len(arrays))
    for i, c in enumerate(clusters):
        for j, a in enumerate(arrays):
            tot[c][j] += a[i]
    return tot
 
 
def wer_ci(clusters, errs, words, B=2000, seed=0):
    """95% percentile interval of a corpus WER, resampling clusters (speakers) with replacement."""
    tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs, words)
    keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(B):
        d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys))
        boots.append(100 * sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) / max(sum(tot[c][1] for c in d), 1))
    return np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
 
 
def paired_contrast(clusters, errs_a, words, errs_b, label_a, label_b, B=2000, seed=0):
    """WER(a) - WER(b) with a paired speaker-cluster bootstrap: the same resampled speakers for both systems."""
    tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs_a, errs_b, words)
    keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(B):
        d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys))
        w = max(sum(tot[c][2] for c in d), 1)
        boots.append(100 * (sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) - sum(tot[c][1] for c in d)) / w)
    boots = np.array(boots)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    p = 2 * min((boots <= 0).mean(), (boots >= 0).mean())
    return {"a": label_a, "b": label_b, "diff": corpus_wer(errs_a, words) - corpus_wer(errs_b, words),
            "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "p": max(p, 1 / B), "clusters": len(keys)}
 
 
def holm(ps, alpha=0.05):
    order, keep = np.argsort(ps), [False] * len(ps)
    for rank, i in enumerate(order):
        if ps[i] <= alpha / (len(ps) - rank):
            keep[i] = True
        else:
            break
    return keep
 
 
def verdict(c, significant):

def quiet_windows(a, limit=30.0, search=5.0, hop=0.2):
    """Cut before `limit` seconds at the quietest `hop`-second patch inside the last `search` seconds of each window."""
    out, i, n, s, h = [], 0, int(limit * SR), int(search * SR), int(hop * SR)
    while len(a) - i > n:
        seg = a[i + n - s:i + n]
        energy = [np.mean(seg[j:j + h] ** 2) for j in range(0, len(seg) - h, h // 4)]
        cut = i + n - s + int(np.argmin(energy)) * (h // 4) + h // 2
        out.append(a[i:cut])
        i = cut
    out.append(a[i:])
    return out
 
 
def speaker_sessions(min_s=40, max_s=100, k=8):
    """Same-speaker concatenations (0.4 s gaps) from the sampled clips of both splits, longest speakers first."""
    by = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for split in ("other", "clean"):
        for c in EN[split]:
            by[c["spk"]].append(c)
    out, gap = [], np.zeros(int(0.4 * SR), np.float32)
    for spk, cs in sorted(by.items(), key=lambda kv: -sum(c["dur"] for c in kv[1])):
        parts, used, total = [], [], 0
        for c in cs:
            if total + c["dur"] + 0.4 > max_s:
                break
            parts += [c["audio"], gap]
            used.append(c)
            total += c["dur"] + 0.4
        if total >= min_s:
            out.append({"spk": spk, "clips": used, "audio": np.concatenate(parts), "ref": " ".join(c["ref"] for c in used), "dur": total})
        if len(out) == k:
            break
    return out

def auroc(scores, labels):
    """Probability that a random positive scores above a random negative (Mann-Whitney)."""
    pos = [s for s, l in zip(scores, labels) if l]
    neg = [s for s, l in zip(scores, labels) if not l]
    if not pos or not neg:
        return float("nan")
    order = sorted((s, i) for i, s in enumerate(scores))
    ranks, i = {}, 0
    while i < len(order):
        j = i
        while j + 1 < len(order) and order[j + 1][0] == order[i][0]:
            j += 1
        for k in range(i, j + 1):
            ranks[order[k][1]] = (i + j) / 2 + 1
        i = j + 1
    pos_idx = [i for i, l in enumerate(labels) if l]
    return (sum(ranks[i] for i in pos_idx) - len(pos) * (len(pos) + 1) / 2) / (len(pos) * len(neg))

Word times are monotonic on every clip we check, and prepending a two-second silence to twenty clips shifts the first word by a median of 2.000 s.             if tag in ("replace", "delete"):
                out += ref.split()[i1:i2]

    print("   matched wrong    = the next error clip's oracle list, minus every word the target clip actually says")
    print("   distractor (8)   = the 8 most frequent reference words of the whole sample that the target clip does not say")
    print("   distractor (2)   = the same list cut to 2 words, so its size matches the oracle and matched arms\n")
 
    def matched_wrong(i):

                          ("distractor (8)", lambda i: distractor(i, 8)), ("distractor (2)", lambda i: distractor(i, 2))):
        errs, words, ins, recovered, total_kw, bad_kw, bad_kw_base, n_kw = [], [], 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
        for i in idx:

            s, d, ins_i = sdi(c["ref"], NORM_EN(h))
            errs.append(s + d + ins_i)
            words.append(len(c["ref"].split()))
            ins += ins_i
            still_wrong = set(error_words(c["ref"], h))

            total_kw += len(oracle[i])
            if kws and name != "oracle (ceiling)":
                bad_kw += sum(w in NORM_EN(h).split() for w in kws)
                bad_kw_base += sum(w in NORM_EN(base[i]).split() for w in kws)
        arms[name] = (errs, words)
        extra = f"   wrong keywords in the output {bad_kw:3d} (already {bad_kw_base} without biasing)" if name not in ("no keywords", "oracle (ceiling)") else ""

Keyword biasing needs controls, because an oracle that reads the answer looks like a win. The oracle lists the words Whistle got wrong; the matched control uses another clip’s, minus any this clip says. On the 185 clips with errors, the oracle cuts WER from 14.74% to 7.62%, while matched wrong words leave it at 14.82%, a non-significant change. Eight frequent words the clip lacks raise WER 2.05 points. Against the oracle, matched wrong words are 7.20 points worse, significant after Holm correction, so the right words matter.

def clopper_pearson_lower(k, n, alpha=0.05):
    """Exact one-sided 95% lower bound for a binomial proportion, by bisection on the binomial tail."""
    lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
    for _ in range(60):
        p = (lo + hi) / 2
        tail = sum(math.comb(n, j) * p ** j * (1 - p) ** (n - j) for j in range(k, n + 1))
        lo, hi = (p, hi) if tail < alpha else (lo, p)
    return lo

    print("   an empty Whisper output is its no-speech gate, not evidence of quality; an empty Whistle output on real speech would be a miss\n")
    clips = EN["other"][:20]
    spk = [c["spk"] for c in clips]
    words = [len(c["ref"].split()) for c in clips]
    print(f"white noise on {len(clips)} test-other clips, {sum(words)} words, {len(set(spk))} speakers (directional at this n):")
    print(f"{'condition':>14s} | {'Whistle':>8s} {'base greedy':>11s} | WER(base) - WER(Whistle), 95% speaker-cluster CI")
    out = []
    for snr in (None, 20, 10, 5):
        xs = []
        for c in clips:
            if snr is None:
                xs.append(c["audio"])
            else:
                n = rng.standard_normal(len(c["audio"])).astype(np.float32)
                n *= np.sqrt((c["audio"] ** 2).mean() / ((n ** 2).mean() * 10 ** (snr / 10)))
                y = c["audio"] + n
                xs.append((y * min(1, 0.99 / np.abs(y).max())).astype(np.float32))
        e_w = [wer_counts(c["ref"], NORM_EN(W.transcribe(x, language="en")["text"]))[0] for c, x in zip(clips, xs)]
        e_b = [wer_counts(c["ref"], NORM_EN(run_whisper("base", x)[0]))[0] for c, x in zip(clips, xs)]
        c = paired_contrast(spk, e_b, words, e_w, "base", "Whistle")
        label = "clean" if snr is None else f"{snr} dB SNR"
        out.append((label, corpus_wer(e_w, words), corpus_wer(e_b, words)))
        print(f"{label:>14s} | {corpus_wer(e_w, words):7.1f}% {corpus_wer(e_b, words):10.1f}% | {c['diff']:+6.1f} ({c['lo']:+.1f}..{c['hi']:+.1f})")
    print("\n   Whistle's front end keeps roughly 250-3500 Hz while Whisper's covers 0-8 kHz, so the two systems do not see the same")
    print("   noise; this compares them as shipped, and at n = 20 none of the differences is distinguishable from zero.")
    return "; ".join(f"{l}: {w:.0f}% vs {b:.0f}%" for l, w, b in out[1:])
 
 
noise()

Digital silence, two noise levels, and a pure tone all give empty text. For Whisper that is a no-speech gate, not evidence of quality, and an empty Whistle output on speech would be a miss. A real sentence at -30 dBFS comes back word for word from Whistle, though Whisper base writes ‘crazed’ for ‘traced’. At the harshest SNR we ran, white noise lifts WER on 20 test-other clips from 12.4% to 37.1% for Whistle and from 15.2% to 39.9% for Whisper base, and no gap is distinguishable from zero.

@section("11. Speech embeddings: the measured frame rate, and finding a spoken word inside another clip")
def embeddings():
    frames = {}
    for secs in (1, 10, 30):
        v = np.asarray(W.embed(audio_seconds(EN["other"], secs)), np.float32)
        frames[secs] = len(v) // 256
        print(f"{secs:2d} s of audio -> {len(v):7d} floats = {len(v)//256:4d} frames x 256  ({len(v)/256/secs:.1f} frames/s, {1000*secs/(len(v)/256):.1f} ms per frame)")
    fps = frames[10] / 10
    try:
        W.embed(np.zeros(31 * SR, np.float32))
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"31 s -> RuntimeError: {e}")
    print("\nspoken-term search: embed clip A whole, keep the frames under one word's own timestamps as the query (the encoder is")
    print("non-causal, so those frames carry context), slide the query over clip B's frames with a cosine score. Pool: the first 120")
    print("test-other clips; words of 5+ letters and 0.25 s+, first two occurrences in different clips; a hit is a peak within 0.3 s.")
    clips = [c for c in EN["other"][:120]]
    key = lambda w: re.sub(r"[^a-z']", "", w.lower())
    occurrences = collections.defaultdict(list)
    for i, c in enumerate(clips):
        for w in W.transcribe(c["audio"], language="en", word_timestamps=True)["words"]:
            if len(key(w["word"])) >= 5 and w["end"] - w["start"] >= 0.25:
                occurrences[key(w["word"])].append((i, w["start"], w["end"]))
    pairs = [(k, o[0], o[1]) for k, o in occurrences.items() if len(o) >= 2 and o[0][0] != o[1][0]]
    cache = {}
 
    def frames_of(i):
        if i not in cache:
            v = np.asarray(W.embed(clips[i]["audio"]), np.float32).reshape(-1, 256)
            cache[i] = v / (np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8)
        return cache[i]
    hits = n = 0
    chance, tol = [], 0.3
    for k, (ia, sa, ea), (ib, sb, eb) in pairs[:60]:
        q = frames_of(ia)[int(sa * fps):max(int(sa * fps) + 2, int(ea * fps))]
        T = frames_of(ib)
        if len(T) <= len(q):
            continue
        scores = np.array([(q * T[j:j + len(q)]).sum(1).mean() for j in range(len(T) - len(q) + 1)])
        peak = (scores.argmax() + len(q) / 2) / fps
        hit = sb - tol <= peak <= eb + tol
        hits += hit
        n += 1
        chance.append((eb - sb + 2 * tol) / clips[ib]["dur"])
        if n <= 3:
            print(f"   {k!r:14s} query {ea-sa:.2f} s from clip {ia:3d} -> peak at {peak:5.2f} s in clip {ib:3d}; the word is spoken at {sb:.2f}-{eb:.2f} s: {'hit' if hit else 'miss'}")
    print(f"   {hits}/{n} peaks inside the target word (+-{tol} s); a random position would land there about {100*np.mean(chance):.0f}% of the time")
    print("   the encoder output is a content representation at frame level; it is not a speaker or sentence embedding")
    return f"{fps:.1f} frames/s x 256 floats; spoken-term search {hits}/{n} hits (chance ~{100*np.mean(chance):.0f}%)"
 
 
embeddings()

Frame rate is measured because the search maps frames to seconds. A ten-second clip yields 25 frames a second, each a 256-float vector, and clips past the embedding limit raise a RuntimeError. We embed a clip whole, since its frames see both sides, and slide one word’s frames across another clip by cosine score. The peak lands within 0.3 s of the word on 32 of 34 pairs of words with five or more letters, where chance gives about 17%. The output is frame-level content, not a sentence embedding.

INTENTS = {"abroad": "Using the card or account while travelling or abroad",
           "address": "Change, update or confirm the postal address on the account",
           "app_error": "The banking app or website shows an error or does not work",
           "atm_limit": "The daily ATM cash withdrawal limit",

N_MINDS = 200
 
 
@section("12. From speech to a tool call: Whistle transcripts into Needle 3 on MInDS-14 banking requests")
def speech_to_tools():
    tools = [{"name": n, "description": d, "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}} for n, d in INTENTS.items()]
    print(f"14 tools, one per MInDS-14 intent, descriptions fixed before the first call (sha256 {hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(tools).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]})")
    first = page("PolyAI/minds14", "en-US", "train", 0, 1)
    names = next(f for f in first["features"] if f["name"] == "intent_class")["type"]["names"]
    assert names == list(INTENTS), names
    rows = all_rows("PolyAI/minds14", "en-US", "train")
    sample = random.Random(SEED).sample(rows, N_MINDS)
    clips, too_long = [], 0
    for r in sample:
        audio, h = load_audio(r)        # 8 kHz telephone wav, resampled to 16 kHz by load_audio
        MANIFEST.setdefault("minds14", []).append([r["path"], h])
        if len(audio) / SR > MAX_CLIP_S:   # the same pre-declared filter as step 2: the engine refuses longer clips
            too_long += 1
            continue
        clips.append({"audio": audio, "ref": r["transcription"], "intent": names[r["intent_class"]], "dur": len(audio) / SR})
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    hyps = [W.transcribe(c["audio"], language="en")["text"] for c in clips]
    tw = time.perf_counter() - t0
    e, n = zip(*[wer_counts(NORM_EN(c["ref"]), NORM_EN(h)) for c, h in zip(clips, hyps)])
    json.dump(MANIFEST, open("manifest.json", "w"))
    print(f"{len(clips)} of the {N_MINDS} sampled clips ({len(rows)} rows in the split; {too_long} dropped for exceeding {MAX_CLIP_S:.0f} s; "
          f"{sum(c['dur'] for c in clips)/60:.1f} min of 8 kHz telephone speech): Whistle WER {corpus_wer(e, n):.1f}% "
          f"against the casual MInDS-14 transcriptions, {1000*tw/len(clips):.0f} ms per clip")
    for c, h in list(zip(clips, hyps))[:2]:
        print(f"   [{c['intent']}] ref: {c['ref'][:72]}\n   {' ' * (len(c['intent']) + 2)} hyp: {h[:72]}")
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    agent = needle.Needle(tools=tools, auto_date=False)   # no date fact in the prompt, so the result does not depend on the clock
    print(f"\nNeedle 3 loaded in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f} s into the same engine; Whistle stays loaded beside it")
 
    def route(texts):
        out = []
        for t in texts:
            r = agent.complete(t)
            agent.reset()
            calls = [c["name"] for c in r.get("function_calls", [])]
            out.append((calls[0] if calls else None, r.get("confidence") or 0.0, r.get("peak_ram_mb")))
        return out
    truth = [c["intent"] for c in clips]
    res = {}
    for label, texts in (("reference transcripts", [c["ref"] for c in clips]), ("Whistle transcripts", hyps)):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        res[label] = route(texts)
        right = np.array([p == y for (p, _, _), y in zip(res[label], truth)])
        conf = np.array([c for _, c, _ in res[label]])
        print(f"   routing from {label:21s}: {100*right.mean():.1f}% correct, {sum(p is None for p, _, _ in res[label])} refusals, "
              f"{1000*(time.perf_counter()-t0)/len(texts):.0f} ms/call, confidence when right {conf[right].mean():.2f} vs wrong {conf[~right].mean():.2f}")
    a = [p == y for (p, _, _), y in zip(res["reference transcripts"], truth)]
    b = [p == y for (p, _, _), y in zip(res["Whistle transcripts"], truth)]
    only_ref, only_wh = sum(x and not y for x, y in zip(a, b)), sum(y and not x for x, y in zip(a, b))
    m = only_ref + only_wh
    p_mc = min(1.0, 2 * sum(math.comb(m, j) for j in range(min(only_ref, only_wh) + 1)) / 2 ** m) if m else 1.0
    print(f"   discordant clips: right only from the reference text {only_ref}, right only from Whistle's text {only_wh} (exact McNemar p = {p_mc:.2f})")
    conf = collections.Counter((y, p) for (p, _, _), y in zip(res["Whistle transcripts"], truth) if p != y)
    print("   most common confusions (truth -> call): " + ", ".join(f"{y} -> {p} x{k}" for (y, p), k in conf.most_common(3)))
    off = route([NORM_EN(h) for h in HYP[("other", "Whistle")][:40]])
    print(f"   40 LibriSpeech sentences (off-topic): {sum(p is None for p, _, _ in off)} refused, {sum(p is not None for p, _, _ in off)} given a banking tool call")
    print(f"   peak_ram_mb reported by Needle: {res['Whistle transcripts'][-1][2]} MB (this whole process, Whisper models included). MInDS-14 is public,")
    print("   so training-set overlap cannot be ruled out for either model, and the tool descriptions are ours: the number moves with them.")
    return f"routing {100*np.mean(b):.0f}% right from Whistle's text vs {100*np.mean(a):.0f}% from the reference text; WER {corpus_wer(e, n):.0f}%"
 
 
speech_to_tools()

Whistle transcribes the sampled MInDS-14 banking requests at 31.9% WER against casual reference transcripts. Needle 3 routes each transcript among fourteen tools, one per banking intent, whose descriptions we wrote. The returned function call becomes the route, and a reply with no call counts as a refusal. Routing is right 50.3% of the time from Whistle’s text and 51.8% from reference text, a non-significant gap, so with these descriptions, routing, not transcription, is the limit. Of the off-topic LibriSpeech sentences, 17 are refused, and the rest get a banking tool call.

for claim, measured, v in VERDICTS:
    print(f"  {claim:<48s} {measured:<58s} {v}")
print(f"\nWhisper audio transcribed in this run: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v/60:.1f} min" for k, v in WHISPER_SECONDS.items())
      + f"; hardware {CPU}")
print("""
What to carry over
 - Pin the Hub revisions of whistle.cact, the engine wheel and needle3.cact and print their hashes; both repos replace files in
   place, and the engine version the package wants is in needle.agent.fetch.ENGINE_VERSIONS, not in the package version.
 - Score with the same normalizer on both sides of each comparison, sample with a fixed seed, cluster the bootstrap by speaker.
 - Say which Whisper you compared against: greedy (the package default) and beam search (the paper's numbers) differ.
 - Keep a single transcribe() call under 30 s; cut longer audio yourself (quiet points worked best on this clip) or use stream().
 - Word probability is a usable error signal, keyword biasing has a ceiling, embeddings are content frames.
Where to go next
 - pip install "cactus-needle[mic,compare]" then needle whistle compare clip.wav runs one clip through Whistle, Whisper and Moonshine.
 - needle download  fetches the engine for macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, RISC-V, MIPS, the browser or WASI; the native
   runner takes --model needle3.cact --model whistle.cact --tools tools.json --audio clip.wav for audio-to-tool-calls in one call.
 - The weights also ship as safetensors, and fine-tuning for new languages is being discussed in the repository's issues.
 - Docs: cactuscompute.com/whistle    Code: github.com/cactus-compute/needle    Weights: huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/whistle
""")

The summary prints each section’s one-line result, then the five published-claim verdicts, where only test-other against greedy Whisper base favors Whistle. It also reports the audio Whisper transcribed, 18.4 minutes for tiny and 68.7 for base, and all 13 cells ran without failure. The habits to carry over are pinning Hub revisions, fixing the seed, scoring both sides with one normalizer, and naming the Whisper decoder.

In conclusion, on an Apple M4 CPU, Whistle scored 10.47% on the test-other sample, near the published full-split 10.49, quoted, not measured. It beat greedy Whisper base by 2.19 points on the paired subset, while beam search, test-clean, and pooled MLS showed no significant gap. It ran 5.7 times faster than greedy base on a ten-second clip. Streaming with one-second chunks committed words a median 1.68 s after they end, with no significant loss. The 30 s limit matters most: the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, so split it or stream. These are one-run samples, and no single clip or small set can settle a claim.

items.title: Wait: Your autonomous Tesla won't drive everywhere just yet
items.summary: Tesla said that it expects to release unsupervised FSD around Q2 2027. Harald Tittel/picture alliance via Getty Images Tesla's Full Self-Driving feature still requires drivers to pay attention to the road. During its Q3 earnings call, the company said unsupervised FSD for personal cars is coming in 2027. The catch? Your Tesla must remain within the company's Robotaxi geofences. When I reviewed Tesla's Full Self-Driving software in January, I hailed it as an "impressive" driver-assistance feature that left me wanting more. I dreamed of being able to flip the autonomous driving system on whenever I make my routine 400-mile trip from San Francisco to Los Angeles — kick my feet up, listen to music, and ideally fall asleep without having to supervise the road. That's been part of Tesla's ultimate pitch for the future. "With autonomy, you get your time back," Elon Musk has said. And the pitch may soon come true. Just don't expect to make long self-driven road trips quite yet. On Wednesday, during Tesla's Q3 earnings call, Ashok Elluswamy , the company's VP of AI, painted a more modest picture of what FSD unsupervised will look like for a personal car — at least at first. Elluswamy said unsupervised FSD is coming "somewhere around Q2 next year" for privately owned Teslas, with the rollout of FSD V15. The caveat is that it will only be operable in areas where Tesla already operates its Robotaxi service, which represents a small fraction of square miles for the total number of Teslas on US roads. The Robotaxi platform is available in parts of seven metropolitan regions: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, and the San Francisco Bay Area. In the Bay Area, all Tesla robotaxis are supervised by a human operator. "The only additional requirement is to make sure that, for example, the customer Model Ys can be part of the geofences and the fleet management that Tesla has for it to be fully autonomous," Elluswamy said. In other words, your Tesla may be able to drive itself, but only if you're within the zones where Tesla Robotaxi is operating. If you're in Austin, that could cover about 260 square miles of the city, excluding high-speed roadways. That's similar to what other aspiring self-driving car companies have pitched. Tensor, a San Jose-based automaker , aims to sell a luxury sedan that it says can drive itself. However, the self-driving feature will only operate within restricted geofences, the company told Business Insider. Tesla didn't say why it needs to limit the release of unsupervised FSD to geofences at first, although there are likely questions about liability that the company will have to address once it declares, Yes, our technology now lets you take your eyes off the road. Autonomy is a difficult problem to solve after all. During the call, Elluswamy shut down the idea that competitors could catch up to Tesla's FSD. "When they get in the long tail of this problem — it's so long that people don't realize — anyone with a sane mind should not attempt to solve this problem," he said. "It's so difficult." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Sundar Pichai explains how a team of AI agents helps him run the company
items.summary: The Google CEO said he uses AI agents to track Google's model development and internal discussions. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sundar Pichai said he uses AI agents to track Google's model development and internal discussions. The bots summarize updates and monitor how Google's computing resources are used. Pichai said humans still make consequential decisions about resource allocation. Even Google's CEO needs help keeping up with Google. On the Sources podcast released Wednesday, Sundar Pichai described to host Alex Heath how he delegates some of the information-gathering that comes with running the tech giant. “It could easily take me an hour a day to kind of catch up, what's happened in the last 24 hours, right?" Pichai said. "But now I have agents running which summarize and bring that information to me. I can still go deeper, and I do so often." Pichai said that his AI agents give him a way to "understand the model development arc," figure out how Google's computing resources are being used, and follow threads spread across numerous internal chat groups without having to read through every conversation himself. “Similarly, there are agents with telemetry into our compute usage by product area, efficiency, utilization, and giving me inputs and insights, you know," Pichai added. "I think it's made all of us, you know, be better at what we do." That doesn't mean Pichai has handed over the important calls to AI. He said humans — including himself — remain directly involved in consequential decisions about allocating computing resources. Managing agents is becoming a skill in its own right, giving some workers a new set of headaches, from checking the bots' output to preventing them from duplicating work or straying beyond their assignments. Business Insider previously reported that the need to manage agents is making everyone a boss without higher pay. Delegating to bots doesn't necessarily make work easier, either. A Cisco engineering director who manages more than 10 agents told Business Insider that overseeing them involves more task switching and can make work feel more intense without shortening his days. For the Google CEO, however, continuous work is a plus. "So because your agents, they're running in the cloud, they're running 24/7, they have your context, and so they can pick up things where you left off," Pichai said. "It's a continuum there. By the time it's doing that, you would be applying yourself to the next problem and so on." Read the original article on Business Insider

"So because your agents, they're running in the cloud, they're running 24/7, they have your context, and so they can pick up things where you left off," Pichai said. "It's a continuum there. By the time it's doing that, you would be applying yourself to the next problem and so on."

items.title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun
items.summary: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief? In the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange to Taika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat. Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while most older critics vehemently, violently disagree . All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. Nobody knows what the hell love is.”

items.title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
items.summary: We study the 305M-parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (identical except for its final projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its weights. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M-parameter CTC reader over a mix of encoder layers; an adapted system adds 3.1M low-rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M-parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub-word language model. Against Cohere Transcribe Arabic (2.07B parameters), re-run on identical audio, the frozen system trails in word error rate (WER) but is statistically indistinguishable in character error rate (CER) on five of six human-labelled conditions, while running 3.4 times faster on CPU with greedy decoding. The adapted system is statistically indistinguishable in WER on a public Saudi customer-service call (19.20% against 19.27%) and on clean Emirati speech, is significantly better on telephone-coded Emirati speech, has a significantly lower CER on all six conditions of these sets, and beats a 0.6B recogniser fine-tuned on SADA in WER on all six; it still trails Cohere in WER on long-form Saudi speech. On a blind, human-corrected public call-centre sample it ranks 4 of 15 systems, behind three commercial APIs (significantly only one) and ahead of the other self-hostable systems by point estimate. An optimised joint decoder runs it at 139 times real time on one GPU. We also show that references made by correcting machine drafts favour the drafting system. Code and public-set results are released.

items.title: Translation and data ethics
items.summary: This chapter introduces data ethics for translation and discusses a number of ethical issues regarding data. These include issues of copyright, ownership and bias, which apply to all types of data, whereas there are further issues particular to minoritised language communities and those on either side of the digital divide, as data is implicated in power imbalances and dynamics. We close with a discussion of responsibility and regulation, and reflect on the growing attention on data ethics from translation studies researchers.

items.title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
items.summary: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

items.title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
items.summary: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment measures how faithfully a therapist adheres to a treatment protocol, a critical determinant of positive patient outcomes. However, fidelity assessment is bottlenecked by manual expert review, rendering the process labor-intensive and unscalable. To scale therapy supervision and support clinician self-learning, we present an integrated application of large language models (LLMs) that automates psychotherapy fidelity workflows and generates actionable supervisory feedback from authentic, long-form clinical transcripts. We evaluate three open-weight models across multiple task decomposition configurations and reasoning strategies, demonstrating that evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation. Furthermore, we establish the framework's external construct validity on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT), where it reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills. Through a user study that evaluates the generated feedback, mental health experts indicate that the pipeline synthesizes actionable clinical feedback. Ultimately, our work offers a practical, scalable solution toward bridging the community mental health supervision gap.

items.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
items.summary: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

items.title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
items.summary: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.
