items.title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
items.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

items.title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
items.summary: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.

items.title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching
items.summary: Flow matching trains a continuum of velocity regression problems but usually reports a loss averaged over interpolation time, obscuring which regions are limited by intrinsic ambiguity and which remain data-limited. We introduce the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP), $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$, the time-local Bayes-risk floor of velocity prediction, and decompose time-resolved loss as $L_N(t)=\mathcal{A}_v(t)+R(t;N)$, where only the excess term $R(t;N)$ is reducible by more data or a different estimator. For $N$ training samples and a $K$-component mixture in the structured example, we prove two statistical benchmarks. In an intrinsic local-regression benchmark, $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$ enters the time-dependent noise factor of the standard nonparametric rate. In separated isotropic Gaussian mixtures, the Bayes velocity becomes locally affine, and a label-oracle residual-regression benchmark has parametric excess-risk scale $K\mathcal{A}_v(t)/N$, matched within the same separated residual Gaussian-location subproblem. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate this diagnostic through a dense transition sweep, calibrated oracle-to-blind and empirical-proxy audits, and a local controlled time-sampler stress test in which a frozen reducible-error proxy reduces reducible loss while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive sampling. On CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow, guided time sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by $6.78\%$ and global feature Fr\'echet distance (FD) by $23.6\%$, while class-conditional kernel inception distance (KID) shows no improvement. VAP turns an averaged flow-matching objective into a time-resolved diagnostic for locating ambiguity-limited and data-limited regions.

items.title: The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks
items.summary: The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher-student model with a convolutional teacher acting on $P$ input positions with correlation $c$ between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension $D$. For uncorrelated positions ($c = 0$), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly $P$ times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D)$ samples, whereas $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log(D))$ samples are needed with a larger kernel. For $c > 0$, spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with $c$, whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of $c$ and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically.

We address these questions in a teacher-student model with a convolutional teacher acting on $P$ input positions with correlation $c$ between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension $D$. For uncorrelated positions ($c = 0$), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly $P$ times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D)$ samples, whereas $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log(D))$ samples are needed with a larger kernel. For $c > 0$, spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with $c$, whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of $c$ and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically.

items.title: Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence
items.summary: We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator.

items.title: NVIDIA Nsight Python Tutorial: How to Profile GPU Kernels
items.summary:
In this tutorial, we implement on Nsight Python , NVIDIA’s open-source Python interface to its kernel profilers. Instead of running a script under the Nsight Compute command line and digging through a report afterward, we mark the code we care about with nsight.annotate, decorate a benchmark function with nsight.analyze.kernel, and get back a pandas DataFrame of hardware metrics per annotated region, per configuration, and per run. Since version 1.0, the library attaches Nsight Compute to the running Python process, making it usable in Jupyter and Colab, and the upcoming 1.1 release adds an experimental CUPTI backend, explicit tool management, and custom information collectors. We run everything on a free Colab T4: we install a current Nsight Compute next to the one Colab ships, profile a first kernel, decide how many runs a measurement needs, measure what cache and clock control do to the same kernel, sweep matrix sizes in fp32 and fp16 with a derived TFLOP/s metric, use hardware counters to tell compute-bound from memory-bound work, measure kernel fusion in bytes moved, record clocks and temperature per run, compare the CUPTI backend with Nsight Compute, and keep the raw report for deeper analysis. The [cupti] extra is used in step 9. Every profiled function below runs in this same") print(" process; nsight-python starts `ncu --mode attach` on its own PID for each one.") We start by checking the GPU and the profiler. Nsight Python requires the Nsight Compute command-line tool, ncu, at version 2026.2.1 or later, and finds it by looking it up on the PATH. Colab’s GPU image ships an older Nsight Compute. Still, it already has NVIDIA’s CUDA package repository configured, so we install Nsight Compute 2026.3.1 with apt-get, ask dpkg where the ncu launcher landed, and put that directory first on the PATH. We then install Nsight Python, pinned to the commit of the 1.1.0 pre-release this notebook was written against, and the cupti-python package into a separate directory, because it needs a newer CUPTI library than the one Colab’s PyTorch is pinned to. The import order matters: import nsight loads Nsight Compute’s injection library into the Python process, and it can only attach to CUDA work started after that, so nsight must be imported before torch touches the GPU.  Only the kernel launched inside nsight.annotate() is profiled; torch.randn above it is not.") print(" With a single run, StableMeasurement is : one sample has no spread to judge.") return f"fp32 2048 matmul {t / 1e6:.3f} ms ({2 * 2048 ** 3 / (t * 1e-9) / 1e12:.2f} TFLOP/s)" first_profile() The first profile is a single fp32 matrix multiplication. The benchmark function creates its inputs, then wraps only the multiplication in nsight.annotate, so the random-number kernels that build the inputs are not measured. Calling the decorated function starts ncu in attach mode on the notebook’s own process, runs the function, and returns a ProfileResults object whose to_dataframe method gives one row per annotation, configuration, and metric. We print the columns and read the row: the kernel name, the measured gpu__time_duration.sum in nanoseconds with its unit, the number of runs, the GPU name and the clock attributes, and we turn the time into TFLOP/s by hand. The combine_kernel_metrics argument sums the time if cuBLAS splits a multiplication into more than one kernel; with a single run, the StableMeasurement flag is undefined, because one sample has no spread. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def show(df, cols, scale=None, fmt="{:,.2f}"): out = df[cols].copy() for c, f in (scale or {}).items(): out[c] = out[c] * f print(textwrap.indent(out.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: fmt.format(v)), " ")) @nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[1 << 14, 1 << 24], runs=20, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT, combine_kernel_metrics=ADD) def noisy_or_not(n: int) -> None: x = torch.randn(n, device="cuda") y = torch.randn(n, device="cuda") a = torch.randn(2048, 2048, device="cuda") with nsight.annotate("vector add"): _ = x + y with nsight.annotate("matmul 2048"): _ = a @ a @section("3. How many runs? Spread, confidence intervals and the stability flag") def stability(): df = noisy_or_not().to_dataframe() print(" 20 runs per configuration; times in microseconds:
") show(df, ["Annotation", "n", "AvgValue", "StdDev", "CI95_Lower", "CI95_Upper", "RelativeStdDevPct", "StableMeasurement"], scale={"AvgValue": 1e-3, "StdDev": 1e-3, "CI95_Lower": 1e-3, "CI95_Upper": 1e-3}) tiny = df[(df.Annotation == "vector add") & (df.n == 1 << 14)].iloc[0] print(f"

The smallest kernel ({tiny['AvgValue'] / 1e3:.1f} us)" f" varies by {tiny['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}%:") print(" at microsecond scale, launch and clock jitter are a large share of the time. Judge small kernels") print(" with more runs, and compare their confidence intervals rather than single averages.") return f"16K-element add RSD {tiny['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}%; " + \ f"2048 matmul RSD {df[df.Annotation == 'matmul 2048'].RelativeStdDevPct.max():.1f}%" stability() A single measurement says nothing about noise, so the next step runs each configuration twenty times. The DataFrame then carries the mean, the standard deviation, a 95 percent confidence interval, the relative standard deviation in percent, and a StableMeasurement flag, which in the source is simply a relative standard deviation below two percent. We profile vector addition at two sizes, a sixteen-thousand-element one that runs in microseconds and a sixteen-million-element one, alongside a 2048 by 2048 matrix multiplication, and compare how much each varies. The practical rule is to run short kernels more times and compare confidence intervals rather than single averages. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser def make_scale_bench(cache_control, clock_control): @nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[1 << 18, 1 << 24], runs=10, cache_control=cache_control, clock_control=clock_control, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT, metrics=["gpu__time_duration.sum", "gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second"]) def scale(n: int) -> None: x = torch.randn(n, device="cuda") with nsight.annotate("x * 2"): _ = x * 2.0 return scale @section("4. Cache and clock control: two defaults that change the answer") def cache_and_clocks(): rows = [] for cache in ("all", "none"): for clock in ("none", "base"): try: df = make_scale_bench(cache, clock)().to_dataframe() except Exception as e: print(f" cache_control={cache!r}, clock_control={clock!r}: failed -> {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:120]}") continue t = df[df.Metric == "gpu__time_duration.sum"].set_index("n").AvgValue hz = df[df.Metric == "gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second"].set_index("n").AvgValue for n in t.index: rows.append({"cache_control": cache, "clock_control": clock, "MB": 4 * n / 2 ** 20, "time_us": t[n] / 1e3, "GB/s": 2 * 4 * n / t[n], "SM_MHz": hz[n] / 1e6}) tab = pd.DataFrame(rows) print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"), " ")) print("
 The T4's L2 cache is 4 MB. A 1 MB input stays in L2 between runs unless caches are flushed,") print(" so cache_control='none' measures a warm-cache kernel and 'all' (the default) a cold one.") print(" clock_control='base' locks the SM clock to base frequency for every replay (the plain ncu CLI") print(" default); nsight-python defaults to 'none', so the GPU boosts. SM_MHz is measured per kernel") print(" (gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second). The ComputeClock column is not: it is the device's") print(" rated clock attribute and stays the same whatever the kernel ran at.") globals()["CLOCK_TABLE"] = tab small = tab[tab.MB < 2].set_index(["cache_control", "clock_control"]).time_us return (f"1 MB scale: cold/boost {small.get(('all', 'none'), float('nan')):.1f} us, " f"warm/boost {small.get(('none', 'none'), float('nan')):.1f} us, " f"cold/base {small.get(('all', 'base'), float('nan')):.1f} us") cache_and_clocks() Two profiler defaults determine what a measurement means, and this step measures both on the same kernel: scaling a vector by two. cache_control decides whether caches are flushed before each kernel replay: Nsight Python flushes them by default, so a small input that would otherwise stay in the T4’s 4 MB L2 cache is read from memory every time. clock_control decides whether the GPU clocks are locked: Nsight Python leaves them unlocked by default, while the plain ncu command line locks them to base clocks. We run all four combinations at 1 MB and 64 MB and also collect gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second, which measures the clock the kernel actually ran at. That matters because, as the source shows, the DataFrame’s ComputeClock column is the device’s rated clock attribute rather than a measurement. ") print(textwrap.indent(fp16.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}"), " ")) print("

A derive_metric function receives the measured time, followed by the benchmark’s arguments, and returns a value with its unit, here TFLOP/s, which the DataFrame stores as an extra metric next to the time. The T4’s datasheet peaks are 8.1 TFLOP/s in fp32 and 65 TFLOP/s in fp16 on its tensor cores, which gives the measured numbers a scale. We then run the same sweep with normalize_against set to the fp32 annotation, which divides every AvgValue by the fp32 value of the same configuration. As the source of the transformation shows, only AvgValue is divided: StdDev, the confidence interval, and the Unit column still describe the raw nanosecond measurement, which is easy to misread. Compute-bound or memory-bound? Three metrics from one replayed kernel") def bound(): df = what_limits(4096).to_dataframe() tab = df.pivot(index="Annotation", columns="Metric", values="AvgValue") tab = tab.rename(columns={"gpu__time_duration.sum": "ms", "sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed": "SM % of peak", "dram__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed": "DRAM % of peak"}) tab["ms"] = tab["ms"] / 1e6 tab["limited by"] = np.where(tab["SM % of peak"] > tab["DRAM % of peak"], "compute", "memory") print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}"), " ")) x2 = tab.loc["x * 2 (256 MB)"] gbs = 2 * 4 * 64 * 2 ** 20 / (x2["ms"] * 1e6) print(f"

Passing a list of metrics makes Nsight Compute replay each kernel as many times as it needs to collect them all, and Nsight Python still returns one row per annotation and metric. We collect the duration, the SM throughput, and the DRAM throughput, each as a percentage of the sustained peak, for three kernels of different character: an fp16 matrix multiplication, a scaling of a 256 MB vecto,r and a softmax over 8192 rows of 1024 values, and label each by whichever throughput is higher. For vector scaling, we also compute the effective bandwidth from the bytes it must move and the measured time, and compare it against the T4’s 320 GB/s datasheet peak and the DRAM percentage Nsight Compute reports. Kernel fusion, measured in bytes: combine_kernel_metrics") def fused(): n = 32 * 2 ** 20 try: fusion_without_combine(n) print(" (the unfused expression profiled without combine_kernel_metrics)") except Exception as e: print(f" Profiled without combine_kernel_metrics, the unfused expression raises:
 {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0][:200]}
") df = fusion(n).to_dataframe() tab = df.pivot(index="Annotation", columns="Metric", values="AvgValue") tab = pd.DataFrame({"ms": tab["gpu__time_duration.sum"] / 1e6, "MB read": tab["dram__bytes_read.sum"] / 2 ** 20, "MB written": tab["dram__bytes_write.sum"] / 2 ** 20}) print(f" {n:,} float32 elements per tensor (128 MB each); metrics summed over the kernels in each region:
") print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"), " ")) u, f = tab.loc["a + b * c (unfused)"], tab.loc["torch.addcmul (fused)"] print(f"
 The unfused version writes b * c to memory and reads it back: {u['MB read'] + u['MB written']:,.0f} MB of") print(f" traffic against {f['MB read'] + f['MB written']:,.0f} MB, and {u['ms'] / f['ms']:.2f}x the time.") return f"fusion: {u['ms'] / f['ms']:.2f}x faster, {(u['MB read'] + u['MB written']) / (f['MB read'] + f['MB written']):.2f}x less traffic" fused() Kernel fusion is usually described in terms of time; here we measure it in bytes. The expression a + b * c in eager PyTorch materializes b * c in memory before adding a, while torch.addcmul computes the same result in one operation. items.summary_html:
In this tutorial, we implement on Nsight Python, NVIDIA’s open-source Python interface to its kernel profilers. Instead of running a script under the Nsight Compute command line and digging through a report afterward, we mark the code we care about with nsight.annotate, decorate a benchmark function with nsight.analyze.kernel, and get back a pandas DataFrame of hardware metrics per annotated region, per configuration, and per run. Since version 1.0, the library attaches Nsight Compute to the running Python process, making it usable in Jupyter and Colab, and the upcoming 1.1 release adds an experimental CUPTI backend, explicit tool management, and custom information collectors. We run everything on a free Colab T4: we install a current Nsight Compute next to the one Colab ships, profile a first kernel, decide how many runs a measurement needs, measure what cache and clock control do to the same kernel, sweep matrix sizes in fp32 and fp16 with a derived TFLOP/s metric, use hardware counters to tell compute-bound from memory-bound work, measure kernel fusion in bytes moved, record clocks and temperature per run, compare the CUPTI backend with Nsight Compute, and keep the raw report for deeper analysis.

import os
import sys
import glob
import json
import time
import shutil
import textwrap
import traceback
import subprocess
 
RESULTS = {}
 
 
def banner(title):
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)
 
 
def section(name):
    def wrap(fn):
        def run(*a, **kw):
            banner(name)
            try:
                out = fn(*a, **kw)
                RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok"
                return out
            except Exception as e:
                RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0][:160]}"
                print(f"\n[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                traceback.print_exc(limit=3)
                return None
        return run
    return wrap
 
 
def sh(cmd):
    """Run a shell command and return its stdout, stripped."""
    return subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
 
 
banner("1. Install a current Nsight Compute next to Colab's, then import nsight before CUDA")
print(f"  GPU: {sh('nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,memory.total,compute_cap --format=csv,noheader')}")
preinstalled = shutil.which("ncu")
print(f"  ncu already on PATH: {preinstalled} -> {sh('ncu --version | tail -1') if preinstalled else 'none'}")
 
# nsight-python needs Nsight Compute 2026.2.1 or newer. Colab ships an older ncu, but its image already
# carries NVIDIA's CUDA apt repository, so a current release is one apt-get away. It installs into
# /opt/nvidia/nsight-compute// and leaves the preinstalled one untouched.
subprocess.run("apt-get update -qq > /tmp/ncu_install.log 2>&1", shell=True)
for NCU_VERSION in ("2026.3.1", "2026.2.1"):
    if subprocess.run(f"apt-get install -y -qq nsight-compute-{NCU_VERSION} >> /tmp/ncu_install.log 2>&1",
                      shell=True).returncode == 0:
        break
else:
    print(sh("tail -5 /tmp/ncu_install.log"))
    raise RuntimeError("could not install Nsight Compute 2026.2.1+ from NVIDIA's apt repository")
# ask dpkg where the package put the ncu launcher rather than assuming /opt/nvidia/nsight-compute//
ncu_paths = sh(f"dpkg -L nsight-compute-{NCU_VERSION} | grep -E '/ncu$'").split()
if not ncu_paths:
    raise RuntimeError(f"dpkg lists no ncu executable in nsight-compute-{NCU_VERSION}")
NCU_DIR = os.path.dirname(min(ncu_paths, key=len))  # the top-level launcher, not a per-platform copy
os.environ["PATH"] = NCU_DIR + os.pathsep + os.environ["PATH"]  # nsight-python looks ncu up on PATH
print(f"  installed: {shutil.which('ncu')} -> {sh('ncu --version | tail -1')}")
 
# nsight-python 1.1.0 (CUPTI backend, tool APIs, info collectors) is tagged but not yet on PyPI;
# pin the commit this notebook was written against. The [cupti] extra is used in step 9.
NSIGHT_COMMIT = "bb96db4260b1823d86ecab9acfed0646d7af79ad"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q",
                f"nsight-python @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/nsight-python@{NSIGHT_COMMIT}"], check=True)
# The CUPTI backend needs cupti-python 13.4, which wants a newer libcupti than Colab's torch is pinned to.
# Install it into a separate directory that only step 9's child process puts on its path.
CUPTI_DIR = "/content/cupti_env"
CUPTI_EXTRA = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "--target", CUPTI_DIR, "--no-deps",
                              "cupti-python>=13.4.0", "nvidia-cuda-cupti~=13.4", "pyelftools"]).returncode == 0
 
import nsight  # activates Nsight Compute's injection library: must come before anything initializes CUDA
from nsight.collection import ncu as ncu_backend
 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
 
SILENT = nsight.VerbosityLevel.SILENT
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 30)
print(f"  nsight-python {nsight.__version__} | active tool: {nsight.get_active_tool()}"
      f" | injection error at import: {ncu_backend.injection_load_error}")
print(f"  torch {torch.__version__} (CUDA {torch.version.cuda}) | {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}"
      f" | cupti-python installed: {CUPTI_EXTRA}")
print("\n  Order matters: `import nsight` loads Nsight Compute into this Python process, and it can only")
print("  attach to CUDA work started after that. Every profiled function below runs in this same")
print("  process; nsight-python starts `ncu --mode attach` on its own PID for each one.")

We start by checking the GPU and the profiler. Nsight Python requires the Nsight Compute command-line tool, ncu, at version 2026.2.1 or later, and finds it by looking it up on the PATH. Colab’s GPU image ships an older Nsight Compute. Still, it already has NVIDIA’s CUDA package repository configured, so we install Nsight Compute 2026.3.1 with apt-get, ask dpkg where the ncu launcher landed, and put that directory first on the PATH. We then install Nsight Python, pinned to the commit of the 1.1.0 pre-release this notebook was written against, and the cupti-python package into a separate directory, because it needs a newer CUPTI library than the one Colab’s PyTorch is pinned to. The import order matters: import nsight loads Nsight Compute’s injection library into the Python process, and it can only attach to CUDA work started after that, so nsight must be imported before torch touches the GPU.

ADD = lambda x, y: x + y   # sums a metric if cuBLAS splits one matmul into several kernels
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(thermal_mode="off", combine_kernel_metrics=ADD)
def first_matmul(n: int) -> None:
    a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    b = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    with nsight.annotate("matmul"):
        _ = a @ b
 
 
@section("2. Profile one kernel: what a ProfileResults row contains")
def first_profile():
    df = first_matmul(2048).to_dataframe()
    print(f"\n  to_dataframe() columns: {list(df.columns)}\n")
    r = df.iloc[0]
    t = float(r["AvgValue"])
    print(f"  annotation {r['Annotation']!r}, n = {r['n']}, kernel {r['Kernel']}")
    print(f"  {r['Metric']} = {t:,.0f} {r['Unit']}  (runs {r['NumRuns']}, stable: {r['StableMeasurement']})")
    print(f"  GPU {r['GPU']}, ComputeClock {r['ComputeClock']}, MemoryClock {r['MemoryClock']}")
    print(f"  -> {2 * 2048 ** 3 / (t * 1e-9) / 1e12:.2f} TFLOP/s for a 2048 x 2048 fp32 matmul")
    print("\n  Only the kernel launched inside nsight.annotate() is profiled; torch.randn above it is not.")
    print("  With a single run, StableMeasurement is : one sample has no spread to judge.")
    return f"fp32 2048 matmul {t / 1e6:.3f} ms ({2 * 2048 ** 3 / (t * 1e-9) / 1e12:.2f} TFLOP/s)"
 
 
first_profile()

The first profile is a single fp32 matrix multiplication. The benchmark function creates its inputs, then wraps only the multiplication in nsight.annotate, so the random-number kernels that build the inputs are not measured. Calling the decorated function starts ncu in attach mode on the notebook’s own process, runs the function, and returns a ProfileResults object whose to_dataframe method gives one row per annotation, configuration, and metric. We print the columns and read the row: the kernel name, the measured gpu__time_duration.sum in nanoseconds with its unit, the number of runs, the GPU name and the clock attributes, and we turn the time into TFLOP/s by hand. The combine_kernel_metrics argument sums the time if cuBLAS splits a multiplication into more than one kernel; with a single run, the StableMeasurement flag is undefined, because one sample has no spread.

def show(df, cols, scale=None, fmt="{:,.2f}"):
    out = df[cols].copy()
    for c, f in (scale or {}).items():
        out[c] = out[c] * f
    print(textwrap.indent(out.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: fmt.format(v)), "  "))
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[1 << 14, 1 << 24], runs=20, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT,
                       combine_kernel_metrics=ADD)
def noisy_or_not(n: int) -> None:
    x = torch.randn(n, device="cuda")
    y = torch.randn(n, device="cuda")
    a = torch.randn(2048, 2048, device="cuda")
    with nsight.annotate("vector add"):
        _ = x + y
    with nsight.annotate("matmul 2048"):
        _ = a @ a
 
 
@section("3. How many runs? Spread, confidence intervals and the stability flag")
def stability():
    df = noisy_or_not().to_dataframe()
    print("  20 runs per configuration; times in microseconds:\n")
    show(df, ["Annotation", "n", "AvgValue", "StdDev", "CI95_Lower", "CI95_Upper", "RelativeStdDevPct",
              "StableMeasurement"], scale={"AvgValue": 1e-3, "StdDev": 1e-3, "CI95_Lower": 1e-3, "CI95_Upper": 1e-3})
    tiny = df[(df.Annotation == "vector add") & (df.n == 1 << 14)].iloc[0]
    print(f"\n  StableMeasurement is simply RelativeStdDevPct < 2. The smallest kernel ({tiny['AvgValue'] / 1e3:.1f} us)"
          f" varies by {tiny['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}%:")
    print("  at microsecond scale, launch and clock jitter are a large share of the time. Judge small kernels")
    print("  with more runs, and compare their confidence intervals rather than single averages.")
    return f"16K-element add RSD {tiny['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}%; " + \
        f"2048 matmul RSD {df[df.Annotation == 'matmul 2048'].RelativeStdDevPct.max():.1f}%"
 
 
stability()

A single measurement says nothing about noise, so the next step runs each configuration twenty times. The DataFrame then carries the mean, the standard deviation, a 95 percent confidence interval, the relative standard deviation in percent, and a StableMeasurement flag, which in the source is simply a relative standard deviation below two percent. We profile vector addition at two sizes, a sixteen-thousand-element one that runs in microseconds and a sixteen-million-element one, alongside a 2048 by 2048 matrix multiplication, and compare how much each varies. The practical rule is to run short kernels more times and compare confidence intervals rather than single averages.

def make_scale_bench(cache_control, clock_control):
    @nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[1 << 18, 1 << 24], runs=10, cache_control=cache_control,
                           clock_control=clock_control, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT,
                           metrics=["gpu__time_duration.sum", "gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second"])
    def scale(n: int) -> None:
        x = torch.randn(n, device="cuda")
        with nsight.annotate("x * 2"):
            _ = x * 2.0
    return scale
 
 
@section("4. Cache and clock control: two defaults that change the answer")
def cache_and_clocks():
    rows = []
    for cache in ("all", "none"):
        for clock in ("none", "base"):
            try:
                df = make_scale_bench(cache, clock)().to_dataframe()
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"  cache_control={cache!r}, clock_control={clock!r}: failed -> {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:120]}")
                continue
            t = df[df.Metric == "gpu__time_duration.sum"].set_index("n").AvgValue
            hz = df[df.Metric == "gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second"].set_index("n").AvgValue
            for n in t.index:
                rows.append({"cache_control": cache, "clock_control": clock, "MB": 4 * n / 2 ** 20,
                             "time_us": t[n] / 1e3, "GB/s": 2 * 4 * n / t[n], "SM_MHz": hz[n] / 1e6})
    tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"), "  "))
    print("\n  The T4's L2 cache is 4 MB. A 1 MB input stays in L2 between runs unless caches are flushed,")
    print("  so cache_control='none' measures a warm-cache kernel and 'all' (the default) a cold one.")
    print("  clock_control='base' locks the SM clock to base frequency for every replay (the plain ncu CLI")
    print("  default); nsight-python defaults to 'none', so the GPU boosts. SM_MHz is measured per kernel")
    print("  (gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second). The ComputeClock column is not: it is the device's")
    print("  rated clock attribute and stays the same whatever the kernel ran at.")
    globals()["CLOCK_TABLE"] = tab
    small = tab[tab.MB < 2].set_index(["cache_control", "clock_control"]).time_us
    return (f"1 MB scale: cold/boost {small.get(('all', 'none'), float('nan')):.1f} us, "
            f"warm/boost {small.get(('none', 'none'), float('nan')):.1f} us, "
            f"cold/base {small.get(('all', 'base'), float('nan')):.1f} us")
 
 
cache_and_clocks()

Two profiler defaults determine what a measurement means, and this step measures both on the same kernel: scaling a vector by two. cache_control decides whether caches are flushed before each kernel replay: Nsight Python flushes them by default, so a small input that would otherwise stay in the T4’s 4 MB L2 cache is read from memory every time. clock_control decides whether the GPU clocks are locked: Nsight Python leaves them unlocked by default, while the plain ncu command line locks them to base clocks. We run all four combinations at 1 MB and 64 MB and also collect gpc__cycles_elapsed.avg.per_second, which measures the clock the kernel actually ran at. That matters because, as the source shows, the DataFrame’s ComputeClock column is the device’s rated clock attribute rather than a measurement.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
SIZES = [(512,), (1024,), (2048,), (4096,)]
 
 
def tflops(time_ns: float, n: int) -> tuple[float, str]:
    return 2 * n ** 3 / (time_ns * 1e-9) / 1e12, "TFLOP/s"
 
 
def make_precision_body():
    def precision(n: int) -> None:   # a fresh function object for each decorator
        a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
        b = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
        a16, b16 = a.half(), b.half()
        with nsight.annotate("fp32"):
            _ = a @ b
        with nsight.annotate("fp16"):
            _ = a16 @ b16
    return precision
 
 
precision_tflops = nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=SIZES, runs=5, derive_metric=tflops, thermal_mode="off",
                                         verbosity=SILENT, combine_kernel_metrics=ADD)(make_precision_body())
precision_ratio = nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=SIZES, runs=5, normalize_against="fp32", thermal_mode="off",
                                        verbosity=SILENT, combine_kernel_metrics=ADD)(make_precision_body())
 
 
@section("5. A size sweep, a derived TFLOP/s metric, and normalisation")
def precision_sweep():
    df = precision_tflops().to_dataframe()
    tf = df[df.Metric == "tflops"].pivot(index="n", columns="Annotation", values="AvgValue")
    print("  derive_metric=tflops receives (gpu__time_duration.sum, n) and returns (value, 'TFLOP/s'):\n")
    print(textwrap.indent(tf[["fp32", "fp16"]].to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}"), "  "))
    print("\n  T4 datasheet peaks: 8.1 TFLOP/s fp32, 65 TFLOP/s fp16 on tensor cores.")
    rd = precision_ratio().to_dataframe()
    fp16 = rd[rd.Annotation == "fp16"][["n", "AvgValue", "StdDev", "Unit", "Normalized"]]
    print("\n  normalize_against='fp32' divides each AvgValue by the fp32 AvgValue of the same configuration:\n")
    print(textwrap.indent(fp16.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}"), "  "))
    print("\n  Read the row carefully: AvgValue is now a ratio (fp16 time / fp32 time), but StdDev and Unit are")
    print("  still those of the raw nanosecond measurement, because only AvgValue is divided.")
    best = tf.loc[4096]
    return f"n=4096: fp32 {best['fp32']:.2f}, fp16 {best['fp16']:.2f} TFLOP/s"
 
 
precision_sweep()

Next, we sweep the matrix size from 512 to 4096 and run both fp32 and fp16 in one benchmark function, with one annotation per precision. A derive_metric function receives the measured time, followed by the benchmark’s arguments, and returns a value with its unit, here TFLOP/s, which the DataFrame stores as an extra metric next to the time. The T4’s datasheet peaks are 8.1 TFLOP/s in fp32 and 65 TFLOP/s in fp16 on its tensor cores, which gives the measured numbers a scale. We then run the same sweep with normalize_against set to the fp32 annotation, which divides every AvgValue by the fp32 value of the same configuration. As the source of the transformation shows, only AvgValue is divided: StdDev, the confidence interval, and the Unit column still describe the raw nanosecond measurement, which is easy to misread.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
BOUND_METRICS = ["gpu__time_duration.sum",
                 "sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed",
                 "dram__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed"]
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(metrics=BOUND_METRICS, runs=3, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT)
def what_limits(n: int) -> None:
    a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda").half()
    x = torch.randn(64 * 2 ** 20, device="cuda")
    s = torch.randn(8192, 1024, device="cuda")
    with nsight.annotate("fp16 matmul 4096"):
        _ = a @ a
    with nsight.annotate("x * 2 (256 MB)"):
        _ = x * 2.0
    with nsight.annotate("softmax 8192x1024"):
        _ = torch.softmax(s, dim=-1)
 
 
@section("6. Compute-bound or memory-bound? Three metrics from one replayed kernel")
def bound():
    df = what_limits(4096).to_dataframe()
    tab = df.pivot(index="Annotation", columns="Metric", values="AvgValue")
    tab = tab.rename(columns={"gpu__time_duration.sum": "ms",
                              "sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed": "SM % of peak",
                              "dram__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed": "DRAM % of peak"})
    tab["ms"] = tab["ms"] / 1e6
    tab["limited by"] = np.where(tab["SM % of peak"] > tab["DRAM % of peak"], "compute", "memory")
    print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}"), "  "))
    x2 = tab.loc["x * 2 (256 MB)"]
    gbs = 2 * 4 * 64 * 2 ** 20 / (x2["ms"] * 1e6)
    print(f"\n  Cross-check: x * 2 moves 2 x 256 MB in {x2['ms']:.2f} ms = {gbs:.0f} GB/s, against the T4's 320 GB/s")
    print(f"  datasheet peak ({100 * gbs / 320:.0f}%); Nsight Compute reports {x2['DRAM % of peak']:.0f}% DRAM throughput.")
    print("  Collecting several metrics makes Nsight Compute replay each kernel once per pass it needs;")
    print("  nsight-python still returns one row per annotation and metric.")
    return f"x*2: {gbs:.0f} GB/s ({x2['DRAM % of peak']:.0f}% DRAM); fp16 matmul SM {tab.loc['fp16 matmul 4096', 'SM % of peak']:.0f}%"
 
 
bound()

Hardware counters tell us why a kernel takes as long as it does. Passing a list of metrics makes Nsight Compute replay each kernel as many times as it needs to collect them all, and Nsight Python still returns one row per annotation and metric. We collect the duration, the SM throughput, and the DRAM throughput, each as a percentage of the sustained peak, for three kernels of different character: an fp16 matrix multiplication, a scaling of a 256 MB vecto,r and a softmax over 8192 rows of 1024 values, and label each by whichever throughput is higher. For vector scaling, we also compute the effective bandwidth from the bytes it must move and the measured time, and compare it against the T4’s 320 GB/s datasheet peak and the DRAM percentage Nsight Compute reports.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
BYTES = ["gpu__time_duration.sum", "dram__bytes_read.sum", "dram__bytes_write.sum"]
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(metrics=BYTES, runs=5, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT,
                       combine_kernel_metrics=lambda x, y: x + y)
def fusion(n: int) -> None:
    a, b, c = (torch.randn(n, device="cuda") for _ in range(3))
    with nsight.annotate("a + b * c (unfused)"):
        _ = a + b * c
    with nsight.annotate("torch.addcmul (fused)"):
        _ = torch.addcmul(a, b, c)
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(runs=1, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT)
def fusion_without_combine(n: int) -> None:
    a, b, c = (torch.randn(n, device="cuda") for _ in range(3))
    with nsight.annotate("a + b * c"):
        _ = a + b * c
 
 
@section("7. Kernel fusion, measured in bytes: combine_kernel_metrics")
def fused():
    n = 32 * 2 ** 20
    try:
        fusion_without_combine(n)
        print("  (the unfused expression profiled without combine_kernel_metrics)")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  Profiled without combine_kernel_metrics, the unfused expression raises:\n    {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0][:200]}\n")
    df = fusion(n).to_dataframe()
    tab = df.pivot(index="Annotation", columns="Metric", values="AvgValue")
    tab = pd.DataFrame({"ms": tab["gpu__time_duration.sum"] / 1e6,
                        "MB read": tab["dram__bytes_read.sum"] / 2 ** 20,
                        "MB written": tab["dram__bytes_write.sum"] / 2 ** 20})
    print(f"  {n:,} float32 elements per tensor (128 MB each); metrics summed over the kernels in each region:\n")
    print(textwrap.indent(tab.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"), "  "))
    u, f = tab.loc["a + b * c (unfused)"], tab.loc["torch.addcmul (fused)"]
    print(f"\n  The unfused version writes b * c to memory and reads it back: {u['MB read'] + u['MB written']:,.0f} MB of")
    print(f"  traffic against {f['MB read'] + f['MB written']:,.0f} MB, and {u['ms'] / f['ms']:.2f}x the time.")
    return f"fusion: {u['ms'] / f['ms']:.2f}x faster, {(u['MB read'] + u['MB written']) / (f['MB read'] + f['MB written']):.2f}x less traffic"
 
 
fused()

Kernel fusion is usually described in terms of time; here we measure it in bytes. The expression a + b * c in eager PyTorch materializes b * c in memory before adding a, while torch.addcmul computes the same result in one operation. We first profile the unfused expression without combine_kernel_metrics to show the error Nsight Python raises when an annotated region contains more than one kernel, then profile both versions with combine_kernel_metrics summing the duration and the DRAM bytes read and written over every kernel in each region, on tensors of 2^25, about 33.5 million, float32 elements.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
import pynvml
 
pynvml.nvmlInit()
NVML = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
 
 
@nsight.experimental.collect(scope=nsight.CollectionScope.ONCE)
def driver_version(*args):
    return pynvml.nvmlSystemGetDriverVersion()
 
 
@nsight.experimental.collect(scope=nsight.CollectionScope.RUN)
def sm_clock_mhz(*args):
    return pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetClockInfo(NVML, pynvml.NVML_CLOCK_SM)
 
 
@nsight.experimental.collect(scope=nsight.CollectionScope.RUN)
def gpu_temp_c(*args):
    return pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetTemperature(NVML, pynvml.NVML_TEMPERATURE_GPU)
 
 
def make_heat_body():
    def heat(n: int) -> None:
        a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda").half()
        with nsight.annotate("fp16 matmul"):
            _ = a @ a
    return heat
 
 
@section("8. Custom info collectors and thermal control (experimental API)")
def collectors():
    out = {}
    for mode in ("off", "auto"):
        bench = nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[4096], runs=30, thermal_mode=mode, thermal_timeout=60,
                                      info_collectors=[driver_version, sm_clock_mhz, gpu_temp_c],
                                      verbosity=SILENT, output_prefix=f"/content/nspy_thermal_{mode}/",
                                      output_csv=True)(make_heat_body())
        t0 = time.time()
        try:
            df = bench().to_dataframe()
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  thermal_mode={mode!r}: failed -> {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).splitlines()[0][:150]}")
            continue
        wall = time.time() - t0
        csvs = sorted(glob.glob(f"/content/nspy_thermal_{mode}/profiled_data-*.csv"))
        raw = pd.read_csv(csvs[-1]) if csvs else pd.DataFrame()
        out[mode] = (df.iloc[0], wall, raw)
        r = df.iloc[0]
        print(f"  thermal_mode={mode!r}: {r['AvgValue'] / 1e6:.3f} ms +/- {r['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}%  "
              f"wall {wall:.0f}s  driver {r['driver_version']}")
    print(f"\n  The collectors became DataFrame columns; RUN-scoped ones were called before every run.")
    if "off" not in out:
        return "info-collector run failed"
    raw = out["off"][2]
    tcol = "Value" if "Value" in raw.columns else raw.columns[-1]
    print(f"  raw per-run CSV columns: {list(raw.columns)}")
    if {"sm_clock_mhz", "gpu_temp_c"} <= set(raw.columns):
        corr = raw[[tcol, "sm_clock_mhz", "gpu_temp_c"]].corr().iloc[0]
        print(f"  over 30 runs: SM clock {raw.sm_clock_mhz.min()}-{raw.sm_clock_mhz.max()} MHz, "
              f"temperature {raw.gpu_temp_c.min()}-{raw.gpu_temp_c.max()} C")
        print(f"  correlation of kernel time with SM clock {corr['sm_clock_mhz']:+.2f}, with temperature {corr['gpu_temp_c']:+.2f}")
    print("\n  thermal_mode='auto' (the default) pauses between runs when the GPU's thermal headroom runs low;")
    print("  the wall-time difference is the price of that, the spread difference what it buys.")
    return "; ".join(f"{m} {out[m][0]['RelativeStdDevPct']:.1f}% RSD in {out[m][1]:.0f}s" for m in out)
 
 
collectors()

Version 1.1 adds custom information collectors, an experimental API for attaching application-specific values to the results. A function decorated with nsight.experimental.collect and a collection scope is called once per session, per configuration, per run or per annotation, and its return value becomes a column. We record the driver version once and read the SM clock and GPU temperature through NVML before every run of a long fp16 multiplication, with output_csv enabled so that the per-run rows are written next to the aggregated ones. We run the benchmark twice, with thermal control off and with the default auto mode, in which Nsight Python pauses between runs when the GPU’s thermal headroom runs low, and compare the spread and the wall-clock time of the two.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
CUPTI_SCRIPT = r'''
import os, json, time
os.environ["NSPY_NCU_INIT_AT_IMPORT"] = "0"     # do not load Nsight Compute in this process
import nsight
nsight.activate(nsight.Tool.CUPTI)
import torch
@nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[512, 1024, 2048, 4096], runs=10, thermal_mode="off",
                       verbosity=nsight.VerbosityLevel.SILENT, combine_kernel_metrics=lambda x, y: x + y)
def matmul(n):
    a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    b = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    with nsight.annotate("matmul"):
        _ = a @ b
t0 = time.time()
df = matmul().to_dataframe()
wall = time.time() - t0
nsight.deactivate()
print(json.dumps({"wall": wall, "rows": df[["n", "AvgValue", "RelativeStdDevPct"]].to_dict("records")}))
'''
 
 
@nsight.analyze.kernel(configs=[512, 1024, 2048, 4096], runs=10, thermal_mode="off", verbosity=SILENT,
                       combine_kernel_metrics=ADD)
def matmul_ncu(n: int) -> None:
    a = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    b = torch.randn(n, n, device="cuda")
    with nsight.annotate("matmul"):
        _ = a @ b
 
 
@section("9. The experimental CUPTI backend, in its own process, against Nsight Compute")
def cupti_vs_ncu():
    t0 = time.time()
    ncu_df = matmul_ncu().to_dataframe().set_index("n")
    ncu_wall = time.time() - t0
    if not CUPTI_EXTRA:
        return f"cupti-python could not be installed; Nsight Compute run took {ncu_wall:.0f}s"
    with open("/content/cupti_matmul.py", "w") as f:
        f.write(CUPTI_SCRIPT)
    env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if k not in ("NVTX_INJECTION64_PATH", "NV_COMPUTE_PROFILER_PERFWORKS_DIR",
                                                             "NV_COMPUTE_PROFILER_IN_PROCESS")}
    env["PYTHONPATH"] = CUPTI_DIR + os.pathsep + env.get("PYTHONPATH", "")
    p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/content/cupti_matmul.py"], capture_output=True, text=True, env=env, timeout=900)
    if p.returncode != 0:
        print(f"  CUPTI run failed (exit {p.returncode}); last lines of its stderr:")
        print(textwrap.indent("\n".join(p.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-8:]), "    "))
        return f"CUPTI backend failed (exit {p.returncode}); Nsight Compute run took {ncu_wall:.0f}s"
    res = next((json.loads(line) for line in reversed(p.stdout.strip().splitlines()) if line.startswith('{"wall"')), None)
    if res is None:
        return f"CUPTI run printed no result; Nsight Compute run took {ncu_wall:.0f}s"
    cu = pd.DataFrame(res["rows"]).set_index("n")
    print(f"  {'n':>5s} {'ncu ms':>8s} {'cupti ms':>9s} {'ratio':>6s} {'ncu RSD%':>9s} {'cupti RSD%':>11s}")
    for n in ncu_df.index:
        a, b = ncu_df.loc[n, "AvgValue"] / 1e6, cu.loc[n, "AvgValue"] / 1e6
        print(f"  {n:5d} {a:8.3f} {b:9.3f} {b / a:6.2f} {ncu_df.loc[n, 'RelativeStdDevPct']:9.1f} {cu.loc[n, 'RelativeStdDevPct']:11.1f}")
    print(f"\n  wall time for 4 sizes x 10 runs: Nsight Compute {ncu_wall:.1f}s, CUPTI {res['wall']:.1f}s"
          f" ({ncu_wall / res['wall']:.1f}x)")
    print("  The two tools are mutually exclusive in one process and Nsight Compute cannot be unloaded, so")
    print("  CUPTI runs in a child process with NSPY_NCU_INIT_AT_IMPORT=0. CUPTI records one execution per")
    print("  launch, with no replay, no cache flush and no clock control: cheaper, and warmer caches.")
    return f"CUPTI {ncu_wall / res['wall']:.1f}x faster to profile; durations within {abs(1 - cu.AvgValue.div(ncu_df.AvgValue)).max():.0%}"
 
 
cupti_vs_ncu()

The CUPTI backend is the other headline feature of 1.1: kernel durations measured through CUPTI’s activity API, without Nsight Compute. The two tools are mutually exclusive within a single process. Nsight Compute cannot be unloaded once active, so we write a small script that sets NSPY_NCU_INIT_AT_IMPORT to 0 before importing nsight, activates the CUPTI tool, profiles the same four matrix sizes, and runs it in a child process with the cupti-python directory on its path. CUPTI supports only the duration metric and records one execution per launch, with no replay, cache flushing, or clock control, so we compare both the durations and the wall-clock cost of profiling against the same benchmark under Nsight Compute.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
@section("10. Keep the evidence: CSVs and the full Nsight Compute report")
def evidence():
    files = sorted(glob.glob("/content/nspy_thermal_off/*"))
    for f in files:
        print(f"  {os.path.basename(f):60s} {os.path.getsize(f) / 1024:9.1f} KB")
    import ncu_report
    rep_path = next((f for f in files if f.endswith(".ncu-rep")), None)
    if rep_path is None:

    print(f"    {len(a0.metric_names())} metrics available in the report for this launch")
    print("\n  output_csv=True writes profiled_data (one row per run) and processed_data (the aggregated")
    print("  DataFrame). The .ncu-rep opens in the Nsight Compute GUI for source-level analysis.")

evidence()

Every profiled call leaves its evidence behind. With an output prefix and output_csv, the directory holds the Nsight Compute report, its log, the per-run profiled_data CSV and the aggregated processed_data CSV. We list the files and open the report with ncu_report, Nsight Compute’s Python report interface, which Nsight Python itself uses: it lists the profiled kernel launches, and each one carries every metric that was collected. The same .ncu-rep file opens in the Nsight Compute interface for source-level analysis.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
banner("SUMMARY")
for name, res in RESULTSitems():
    print(f"  {name:<76s}  {res}")
print("""
What to carry over
 - import nsight first; it loads Nsight Compute into the process before CUDA starts.
 - Annotate exactly the work you mean to measure; one kernel per region unless you pass
   combine_kernel_metrics.
 - Decide cache and clock control on purpose: nsight-python flushes caches and leaves clocks
   unlocked by default, which is not what a plain ncu run does.
 - Use runs and the CI95 / RelativeStdDevPct columns; one run tells you nothing about noise.
 - After normalize_against, only AvgValue is a ratio.
Where to go next
 - Triton and cuTile kernels: examples/07_triton_minimal.py and examples/12_cutile.py.
 - Plots: @nsight.analyze.plot(...) on top of @nsight.analyze.kernel, with row/col panels.
 - Docs: docs.nvidia.com/nsight-python    Code: github.com/NVIDIA/nsight-python
""")

The summary prints the one-line result of each step and the habits worth keeping: import nsight before anything initializes CUDA, annotate exactly the work you mean to measure, choose cache and clock control deliberately, use enough runs and read the confidence intervals, and remember that only AvgValue is normalized. It ends with pointers to the Triton and cuTile examples in the repository and to the plotting decorator.

In conclusion, Nsight Python turns kernel profiling from a separate command-line session into a few lines in the code being measured: a decorator, an annotation, and a DataFrame that carries the measurement, its spread, and its context. Working through it on a Colab T4 also shows where the convenience hides decisions that change the numbers. The profiler has to be newer than the one Colab ships and must be loaded before CUDA starts. Cache flushing and clock locking default to the opposite of what a plain ncu run does; the clock column reports the card’s rating rather than the clock the kernel ran at; normalization divides only the average. Every annotated region is expected to hold exactly one kernel unless you say how to combine them. Once those choices are explicit, the same few lines answer the questions that matter in practice: how stable a timing is, what limits a kernel, what fusion actually saves, and what a cheaper profiler such as the new CUPTI backend gives up for its lower overhead.

items.title: Why Nandan Nilekani-Backed F2A Believes India's Investment Opportunity Lies in Edge AI
items.summary: Deeptech investments are notorious for having long investment cycles. They can take anywhere between 7–12 years from founding to a liquidity event given the intensive R&D and testing phases. This requires specialised patient capital—something not many funds are willing to dabble in. Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A), the investment platform led by Ashish Kumar and anchored by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, is not among them. It recently secured ₹3,000 crore in subscriptions for its growth-stage AI and deeptech fund. Its limited partners have approved increasing the fund’s hard cap to ₹3,500 crore, following demand beyond its available capacity. The fund plans to deploy capital over the next two to three years. It expects to invest in 12–15 companies, with individual cheques of ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore, according to F2A’s announcement. Kumar believes the investor interest reflects growing recognition that Indian AI and deep-tech businesses may follow a different path from companies in Western markets. “The reason is people have bought the story; people have realised that the Indian AI and deeptech companies will not necessarily look exactly similar to what is happening in the West,” he tells AIM. He points to India’s own supply chains and the opportunity to develop companies around local requirements. Kumar also sees a gap in the market for investors willing to back deeptech businesses at the growth stage, when they need substantial capital to expand. Where F2A Plans to Invest F2A plans to allocate around 40% of its investments to physical AI , including semiconductors, advanced materials, robotics, and space technology. Another 40% will go to digital consumer companies using AI, while the remaining 20% will target enterprise tools, including frontier models, databases, and analytics. Kumar describes physical AI as a combination of hardware and software, rather than a category limited to hardware manufacturers. He adds that the software component could take different forms, including models running on a platform or systems designed to improve data storage and memory utilisation. F2A is also looking at companies that could help India build capabilities in strategically important sectors. Kumar identifies communications, security, financial services, healthcare, and food systems as areas where domestic technology businesses could have a role. He acknowledges that complete supply-chain independence is not realistic for any country. Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A), the investment platform led by Ashish Kumar and anchored by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, is not among them. It recently secured ₹3,000 crore in subscriptions for its growth-stage AI and deeptech fund.

Its limited partners have approved increasing the fund’s hard cap to ₹3,500 crore, following demand beyond its available capacity.

The fund plans to deploy capital over the next two to three years. It expects to invest in 12–15 companies, with individual cheques of ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore, according to F2A’s announcement.

Kumar believes the investor interest reflects growing recognition that Indian AI and deep-tech businesses may follow a different path from companies in Western markets.

“The reason is people have bought the story; people have realised that the Indian AI and deeptech companies will not necessarily look exactly similar to what is happening in the West,” he tells AIM.

items.title: A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked
items.summary: Ilya Pavlov / Unsplash Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites . Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline. The Australian Signals Directorate , America’s Cyber Defence Agency , and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed. The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time. What is PHP? PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes. The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites. PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it. A timeline of concerns In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase . The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet. Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web. Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix. In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit. This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready. Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule. Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix. Why does this keep happening? Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding. Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data. Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations . All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital . Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is. What should you do? This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security. For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days. Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning. Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call. Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on. Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening. Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.

items.title: The Closing of the ‘Defenders Window’ Is Nigh
items.summary: At first, the X headlines this morning about the latest AI-powered cybersecurity incident seemed dire. But by the time I had a cup of coffee and began parsing all the cyber jargon, I was reassured that an apparent solution was on its way to plug a major new security hole that could make websites vulnerable to cyberintrusions. Since August, a coalition led by OpenAI has been working to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that undergirds the web. But there was bad news, too: This type of long-simmering response to the latest AI-discovered vulnerabilities may not be viable for much longer. For months, OpenAI has been harping on what it calls the “ defender’s window ”—the critical period of time when cybersecurity experts, armed with advanced AI models, can identify and patch vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them first. The issue is that the gap is rapidly narrowing between cybercapable models from leading U.S. frontier labs and Chinese open-source models, which lack the restrictions U.S. labs impose on their models’ capabilities. Anthropic said as much in a blog post from late September warning that Chinese lab Z.ai ’s GLM-5.3 model only lags the U.S. frontier models by about four months. The good news: The Trump administration has a shiny new organization created for moments just like these. It’s called the Super Intelligence Force, a name that may elicit eyerolls from some of our more jaded readers. Still, I have heard over and over that all the AI industry wants is coordination and clarity from the White House. That, presumably, is what the SI Force will offer, led by heavy hitters including National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and senior Defense Department official Emil Michael . An OpenAI spokesperson told me today that they had briefed several agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, about the PHP vulnerability, as well as briefing Clayton and Michael late last week, representing the first “major engagement” between OpenAI and the SI Force. The spokesperson added that the SI Force provided a central point to coordinate their communication across the broader government. According to a White House official, the SI Force’s work involved helping to put pressure on the “relevant parties” to deploy a vulnerability patch. While the SI Force’s coordination function may not seem terribly ambitious, at least it’s a start. It’s worth remembering that the White House essentially had to reorient its entire AI policy in April with the announcement of Mythos. The arrival of Chinese cybercapable open models could represent a Mythos 2.0 moment. I spoke with one former White House official who told me solutions from even a few months ago, like the July Gold Eagle clearinghouse that allows organizations and government agencies to share and fix software vulnerabilities, might already be outdated. It’s up to the SI Force to create a path forward. The next major internet bug likely won’t have the luxury of a two-month-long defender’s window. Meta’s Performance On Sunday, in a preview of this week’s Meta Platforms earnings report, your regular Briefing columnist, Martin Peers, declared: “If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards.” Martin nailed it on both accounts. On Wednesday afternoon, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivered a bunch of (mostly) good news that had investors in the company purring like kittens. Meta also announced the creation of a new category of common stock that will allow it to raise capital to fund its hefty AI investments without sacrificing Zuckerberg’s control. The highlights: For the third quarter, its revenue grew 26% to $64.6 billion, slightly above what the company had forecast. It’s trimming the losses from its Reality Labs unit. While it showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion rather than the positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion in the year-earlier period, that was due to its AI investments, and the number wasn’t as bad as some analysts had expected. The company’s anticipated capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, while eye-popping, were still within the range it had previously forecast. That was reassuring for investors who’ve gotten spooked in the past by sudden leaps in tech company spending on AI. Perhaps equally comforting were Zuckerberg’s reassurances that investors will see a payoff from some of its most expensive AI initiatives. He described Muse, Meta’s new agent app, as a bona fide hit for the company, one that has gained 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first six weeks on the market—a faster pace of growth than for its Threads app. While Zuckerberg said the product will remain free for most people, he described a number of ways Meta plans to eventually get paid for it, including commerce transaction fees paid by businesses and money power users will pay for access to advanced models and extra tokens. Meta shares rose 2% in after-hours trading. Meta also warned of some potentially expensive new legal costs on the horizon, including from lawsuits related to child safety legal cases. During the third quarter, Meta said, its operating income declined 37% from a year earlier to just under $13 billion, due in large part to a nearly $10 billion charge related to legal proceedings. In August, the company settled a child online safety case with 52 attorneys general for $18.59 billion. And on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Meta did not say when it plans to raise capital through a new equity offering, or how much it might raise. Presumably, that will happen after Jan. 19, the effective date for issuance of the new nonvoting Class C common stock the company announced today. The company’s existing shareholders will receive a dividend of one Class C share for each share of Class A or B common stock they hold. And crucially, when the company raises money in the future with its Class C stock, that won’t dilute Zuckerberg’s voting power. “The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said. —Nick Wingfield Tongue-Tied at Tesla On Tesla’s earnings call, Elon Musk had much less to say on the topic of a potential merger of the EV maker with his other company, SpaceX, than he did Tuesday afternoon on SpaceX’s earnings call. He told investors he had said everything he wanted to on the topic for now. Tesla’s automotive revenues fell 3% to $20.56 billion while its total revenues remained flat at $28 billion compared to a year earlier. Tesla shares fell 3% in after-hours trading. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Electronic Arts plans to shed around 400 jobs, or about 3% of its staff, and shut down its BioWare studio, Bloomberg reported . Microsoft asked shareholders to approve a plan to lower CEO Satya Nadella’s pay by 6% due to falling revenue in its Xbox unit. The company also nominated Stripe co-founder John Collison to its board. Google will stop requiring local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements when it plans to build data centers in their areas. Still, I have heard over and over that all the AI industry wants is coordination and clarity from the White House. That, presumably, is what the SI Force will offer, led by heavy hitters including National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and senior Defense Department official Emil Michael. 

An OpenAI spokesperson told me today that they had briefed several agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, about the PHP vulnerability, as well as briefing Clayton and Michael late last week, representing the first “major engagement” between OpenAI and the SI Force. The spokesperson added that the SI Force provided a central point to coordinate their communication across the broader government. According to a White House official, the SI Force’s work involved helping to put pressure on the “relevant parties” to deploy a vulnerability patch. 

While the SI Force’s coordination function may not seem terribly ambitious, at least it’s a start. It’s worth remembering that the White House essentially had to reorient its entire AI policy in April with the announcement of Mythos. The arrival of Chinese cybercapable open models could represent a Mythos 2.0 moment. I spoke with one former White House official who told me solutions from even a few months ago, like the July Gold Eagle clearinghouse that allows organizations and government agencies to share and fix software vulnerabilities, might already be outdated. It’s up to the SI Force to create a path forward. The next major internet bug likely won’t have the luxury of a two-month-long defender’s window.

Meta’s Performance

On Sunday, in a preview of this week’s Meta Platforms earnings report, your regular Briefing columnist, Martin Peers, declared: “If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards.” Martin nailed it on both accounts. On Wednesday afternoon, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivered a bunch of (mostly) good news that had investors in the company purring like kittens. Meta also announced the creation of a new category of common stock that will allow it to raise capital to fund its hefty AI investments without sacrificing Zuckerberg’s control. 

The highlights: For the third quarter, its revenue grew 26% to $64.6 billion, slightly above what the company had forecast. It’s trimming the losses from its Reality Labs unit. While it showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion rather than the positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion in the year-earlier period, that was due to its AI investments, and the number wasn’t as bad as some analysts had expected. The company’s anticipated capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, while eye-popping, were still within the range it had previously forecast. That was reassuring for investors who’ve gotten spooked in the past by sudden leaps in tech company spending on AI.

Perhaps equally comforting were Zuckerberg’s reassurances that investors will see a payoff from some of its most expensive AI initiatives. He described Muse, Meta’s new agent app, as a bona fide hit for the company, one that has gained 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first six weeks on the market—a faster pace of growth than for its Threads app. While Zuckerberg said the product will remain free for most people, he described a number of ways Meta plans to eventually get paid for it, including commerce transaction fees paid by businesses and money power users will pay for access to advanced models and extra tokens. Meta shares rose 2% in after-hours trading.

Meta also warned of some potentially expensive new legal costs on the horizon, including from lawsuits related to child safety legal cases. During the third quarter, Meta said, its operating income declined 37% from a year earlier to just under $13 billion, due in large part to a nearly $10 billion charge related to legal proceedings. In August, the company settled a child online safety case with 52 attorneys general for $18.59 billion. And on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Meta did not say when it plans to raise capital through a new equity offering, or how much it might raise. Presumably, that will happen after Jan. 19, the effective date for issuance of the new nonvoting Class C common stock the company announced today. The company’s existing shareholders will receive a dividend of one Class C share for each share of Class A or B common stock they hold. And crucially, when the company raises money in the future with its Class C stock, that won’t dilute Zuckerberg’s voting power. “The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said.—Nick Wingfield

Tongue-Tied at Tesla

On Tesla’s earnings call, Elon Musk had much less to say on the topic of a potential merger of the EV maker with his other company, SpaceX, than he did Tuesday afternoon on SpaceX’s earnings call. He told investors he had said everything he wanted to on the topic for now. Tesla’s automotive revenues fell 3% to $20.56 billion while its total revenues remained flat at $28 billion compared to a year earlier. Tesla shares fell 3% in after-hours trading.—Nick Wingfield 

In Other News
  • Electronic Arts plans to shed around 400 jobs, or about 3% of its staff, and shut down its BioWare studio, Bloomberg reported. 
  • Microsoft asked shareholders to approve a plan to lower CEO Satya Nadella’s pay by 6% due to falling revenue in its Xbox unit. The company also nominated Stripe co-founder John Collison to its board.
  • Google will stop requiring local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements when it plans to build data centers in their areas.
